translation_en:
Wang Po, courtesy name Tingrui, was registered in Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the eighteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yanwen; his grandfather, Lu; his father, Zhen; and his mother, née Jiang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Hu, and his wife was née Zhao. He placed seventy-third in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 205th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tang Bi, courtesy name Xiyue, was registered in She County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was fourth in birth order, aged forty-two, and born on the thirteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ziyi, a medical official; his grandfather, Yongji; his father, Bangli; and his mother, née Wang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Yuan, Zuo (a provincial graduate), and Xiang (an Investigating Censor); his younger brother was Tai. His wife was née Yu. He placed 102nd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 200th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Tingzhen, courtesy name Xiaoru, was a native of Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, registered in a military household of the Dahe Central Stationary Guard in that region. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the twentieth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yanzhen; his grandfather, Cunli; and his father, Yi. His legal mother was née Zhou, and his birth mother was née Ma. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Xuan; his younger brother, Cong; and his wife, née Han. He placed sixteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 223rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Yue, courtesy name Zibo, was registered in Linchuan County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was eighth in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the fourteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rongshou; his grandfather, Xuemin, an Investigating Censor; his father, Yi, an Assistant Instructor; and his mother, née Wan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Xu, Fan (䌓), and Zhen; his younger brothers were Ji, Hong, Chun, Jing, Gang, Wei, and Lun. His wife was née Niu. He placed twelfth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 273rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

劉泰〔貫順天府固安縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字世亨，行一，年四十，十月十六日生〕。曾祖文舉，祖奉先，父信，母葛氏。永感下，娶陳氏。順天府鄉試第一百三十五名，會試第五十二名。

韓普〔貫山東兖州府滋陽縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字文博，行二，年二十八，三月二十三日生〕。曾祖景華，祖晟，父惠〔前錄事〕，母程氏。具慶下，兄智〔貢士〕，弟曆，娶孔氏。山東鄉試第三十三名，會試第七十六名。
translation_en:
Chen Hui 陳晦 was a registered native of Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, from a civilian household and a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Daizheng. He ranked second in birth order, was aged twenty-seven, and was born on the fourth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shangqian; his grandfather, La, was a vice commissioner of a capital treasury; his father, Ji, was a school instructor; and his mother was née Lin. His parents and grandparents were deceased. His elder brothers were Dezheng and Yaozheng, and his younger brother was Zhao. He married a woman née Peng. He placed sixth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 108th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hu Xianzong 胡顯宗 was a native of Linhuai County, Fengyang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, registered in an officer household of the Left Yulin Guard, and a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Shirong. He ranked first in birth order, was aged forty-eight, and was born on the eighteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather, Wen, grandfather, Shan, and father, Jian, were all assistant commanders and were each invested with the title General of Manifest Might. His father's former wife, née Chen, and his mother, née Han, were each invested with the title Lady of Respect. His parents and grandparents were deceased. His younger brothers were Shaozong and Jizong. He married a woman née Gao. He placed eleventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 174th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Tai 劉泰 was a registered native of Gu'an County, Shuntian Prefecture, from a civilian household and a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Shiheng. He ranked first in birth order, was aged forty, and was born on the sixteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenju; his grandfather was Fengxian; his father was Xin; and his mother was née Ge. His parents and grandparents were deceased. He married a woman née Chen. He placed 135th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Han Pu 韓普 was a registered native of Ziyang County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, from a civilian household and a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Wenbo. He ranked second in birth order, was aged twenty-eight, and was born on the twenty-third day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jinghua; his grandfather was Sheng; his father, Hui, was a former recorder; and his mother was née Cheng. Both his parents were living. His elder brother, Zhi, was a tribute scholar (gongshi), and his younger brother was Li. He married a woman née Kong. He placed thirty-third in the Shandong Provincial Examination and seventy-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Weng Li, registered in Raoping County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Cundao. Second among his brothers, he was aged thirty-two and was born on the second day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Jiyan, his grandfather Zao, his father Zhu, and his mother née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Ying; his younger brothers were Yu, Xu, Ji, and Qi. His wife was née Chen. He placed fortieth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yuan Mengti, registered in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Benren. Second among his brothers, he was aged fifty and was born on the eighth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Gui, a Supervising Secretary; his grandfather was Zhong, an Honorary Official for Righteousness; and his father was Yingbiao. His father's former wife was née Xie, his mother née Tong, and his stepmother née Ke. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Mengkai; his younger brothers were Mengyi, Shen, Xie, and Xian. His wife was née Wang. He placed forty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 302nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ren Yi, registered in Langzhong County, Baoning Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a military household and was a student of the prefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Xiangzhi. Second among his brothers, he was aged twenty-eight and was born on the fourth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Changsi, his grandfather Chao, his father Rang, a student of the Imperial University, and his mother née Cui. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Wei, and his wife was née Zhu. He placed third in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 221st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Jie, registered in Longzhou, Fengxiang Prefecture, Shaanxi, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Yunde. First among his brothers, he was aged thirty and was born on the seventh day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Xiu; his grandfather was Xuan, a Director of Schools posthumously granted the title of Vice Director; his father was Zhongshi, an Administration Vice Commissioner in the Provincial Administration Commission; and his mother was née Wang, invested with the title Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Kan, Fang, Shen, and Wei. His wife was née Wang. He placed twelfth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 340th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Jiang Pu, registered in Guangde Department in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a National University student specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Xiguang; he was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the thirteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Keming, an Assistant Instructor; his grandfather was Chuqian; and his father was Shao. His father's former wives were Lady Ding and Lady Pan, and his mother was Lady Hu. His father alone was still living. His elder brother was Hong, an Investigating Censor, and his younger brothers were Qing, Shen, Cheng, and Yuan. He married Lady Wang and subsequently Lady Chen. He placed fifth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 166th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Gong, registered in Neijiang County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a civilian household and was a National University student specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Chaoyi; he was third in birth order, aged forty, and born on the third day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Youcai, his grandfather was Zhiming, and his father was Shizong; his mother was Lady Tian. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Bodou and Bochen. He married Lady Zhou. He placed sixty-ninth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 280th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Tinggui, registered in Yifeng County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a military household and was a National University student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Bangqi; he was first in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the eleventh day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bin; his grandfather was Yan, a Clerk; and his father was Qing. His mother was Lady Ouyang. Both parents were still living. His younger brothers were Tingzhang, Tinghuan, Tingwan, and Tingjie. He married Lady Jia. He placed fifty-eighth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 190th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Huan, registered in Tiantai County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was an Added Student of the county school, specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Chongzhong; he was fifth in birth order, aged forty-three, and born on the fifth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yanhua; his grandfather was Sijiang; and his father was Gongquan, an Instructor. His father's former wife was Lady Zhang, and his mother was Lady Huang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ao, Zheng, Duo, and Jian, and his younger brothers were Qian and Lu. He married Lady Zhao. He placed twenty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 197th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Long, registered in a military household in Yushe County, Liao Subprefecture, Shanxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Shichang; he was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the tenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was An, his grandfather Yanhong, and his father Zhong; his mother was née Chai and his stepmother née Ma. His father alone was living. His elder brother was Zhongshan and his younger brother Sheng; his wife was née Gao. He placed twenty-fifth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 126th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Mou Dao, registered in a civilian household in Ba County, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan, was a county school student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Wenzai; he was fifth in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the second day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yinglong, his grandfather Gutai, and his father Ji; his mother was née Huang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Zhongren, Zhongzhi, Zhongxin, and Zhongyi; his wife was née Yang. He placed fourth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 152nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Lian, registered in a military household in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Fangzhen; he was second in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the eleventh day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Deyi, his grandfather Xingsu, and his father Chong, a prefect; his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Guang and his younger brothers Kang and Shu; his wife was née Chen. He placed first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Huaijing, registered in a civilian household in Xinchang County, Ruizhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shiji; he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the sixteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Dehe, his grandfather Weicai, and his father Shouxun; his mother was née Li. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Huaijun and Huaiying, the latter a tribute scholar (gongshi); his wife was née Xiong. He placed thirty-fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 272nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xie Hu 謝湖, courtesy name Yourong, was registered in Haiyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was second in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the twentieth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zilu; his grandfather was Hongyi, an honorary official; his father was Liu, and his mother was née Su. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother Shu was a tribute scholar (gongshi). He married a woman née Wang. He placed fifty-ninth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 320th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Zhen 嚴禎, courtesy name Tingrui, was registered in Xiaogan County, De’an Prefecture, Huguang, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he was third in birth order, aged forty-eight, and born on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zongkui; his grandfather was Shizhong; his father was Min, a county vice magistrate, and his mother was née Zou. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Guang and Ying, and his younger brother was Xiang. He married a woman née Li and subsequently a woman née Che. He placed fifteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 202nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Feng Hao 馮浩, courtesy name Yangzheng, was registered in Jiangpu County, Yingtian Prefecture, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-one, and born on the seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gong; his grandfather was Yanneng; his father was Ming, and his mother was née Di. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Qing, Zhang, Zhan, and Guan. He married a woman née Liu. He placed 104th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Ji 朱璣, courtesy name Wenrui, was a native of Luanzhou, Yongping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was registered in a military household of the Menghua Guard in Yunnan. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was third in birth order, aged forty, and born on the first day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Delin; his grandfather was Cheng; his father was Wang; his father’s former wife was née Zhong, and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Zhen and Xiang, and his younger brother was Ying. He married a woman née Yan. He placed thirtieth in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 349th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Xidan, courtesy name Jingzhe, was registered in a military household in Jingshan County, Anlu Subprefecture, Huguang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked third among his brothers and was forty-four years old, born on the eighteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Siwen, his grandfather Liang, and his father Bozhen; his mother was née Chen. His parents and grandparents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yi and Chang, and his wife was née He. He placed forty-second in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 165th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hua Jin, courtesy name Jizhi, was registered in a civilian household in Wuxi County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked third among his brothers and was thirty years old, born on the twenty-eighth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Liang, his grandfather Jun, and his father Xuan; his mother was née Cai. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yi and Shu, and his younger brothers Xiao and Han; his wife was née Qian. He placed 102nd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 342nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Pan Kai, courtesy name Yizheng, was a native of Liyang County, Yingtian Prefecture, registered in an officer household of the Embroidered-uniform Guard. A student of the military school for the capital guards specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked second among his brothers and was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Guiming, his grandfather Daoxin (posthumously granted the title Commandant of Manifest Fidelity), and his father Yong (a Company Commander); his mother was née Jin (granted the title Lady of Peace). Both parents were living. His elder brother was Xun, and his younger brothers Xiang, Fei, and Zou; his wife was née Song. He placed fifty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 274th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Cunzhong, courtesy name Chengzhi, was registered in a civilian household in Xianju County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked ninth among his brothers and was forty-one years old, born on the twelfth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Siming, his grandfather Wenbin, and his father Yongchao; his father's former wife was née Shen, and his mother was née Yang. His parents and grandparents were deceased. His elder brothers were Cunshang, Mei, Ying, Ci, Ying, Yi, Mu, and Huai, and his younger brothers Liang, Jiu, Ji, Hao, Bu, and Yi; his wife was née Yin. He placed ninety-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Ye Ting 葉鋌, courtesy name Weigang, was from Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, and belonged to a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He was eighth in birth order, aged thirty-seven, and born on the twenty-first day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jun; his grandfather, Zhenyuan; his father, Siyong, an honorary official; and his mother, née Shao. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Xian, an honorary official, and Lang. He married a woman née Huang. He placed eighth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 169th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ren Liangcai 任良才, courtesy name Tingju, was from Pingyao County, Fenzhou, Shanxi, and belonged to a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He was first in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the third day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Xiao; his grandfather, Yi, a district magistrate; and his father, Hui. His father's former wife was née Zhang, his mother was née Fan, and his stepmother was née Ji. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Liangbi, a tribute scholar (gongshi); Liangzuo; Liangqing; Liangjin; Liangyu; and Liangxi. He married a woman née Hu. He placed fortieth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 345th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hu Ang 胡昂, courtesy name Shiju, was from Guichi County, Chizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and belonged to a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Odes. He was second in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the eleventh day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Zhongming; his grandfather, Yonghai; his father, Zhongli; and his mother, née Zhu. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brother was Sheng, and his younger brothers were Jingbing and Mian. He married a woman née Qian. He placed seventy-fifth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Shize 張時澤, courtesy name Jimin, was from Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and belonged to a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Rites. He was ninth in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the twenty-fifth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Menglian; his grandfather, Xi; his father, Tingyu; and his mother, née Shao. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Run, a registrar, and his younger brother was Jian. He married a woman née Wang. He placed seventy-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 121st in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xing Lin, registered in an artisan household in Xiangling County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Shiwang; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-five sui, born on the fourteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jingli; his grandfather, Maozheng, was posthumously granted the title of Chancellor of the Directorate of Education; his father, Rang, was Left Vice Minister of Rites; and his mother, née Liang, held the title of Respectful Lady. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother, Zhen, was a student of the Directorate of Education; his younger brothers were Pei and Xi. His wife was née Wang. He placed twenty-fifth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 304th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Lan, registered in a military household in Deqing Subprefecture, Zhaoqing Prefecture, Guangdong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Dongzhi; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-five sui, born on the twenty-first day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Zongyuan; his grandfather, Fu, was a District Magistrate; his father was Zuan; his mother was née Deng; and his stepmother was née Kong. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Han and Ying, and his wife was née Li. He placed fifteenth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 148th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Ju, registered in a medical household in Wangjiang County, Anqing Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Liangpei; he ranked tenth among his brothers and was thirty-eight sui, born on the first day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Huaqing; his grandfather was Zhenlong; and his father, Jing, was granted the title of Supervising Secretary. His father's former wife, née Dong, and his mother, née Li, were both posthumously granted the title of Lady; his stepmother was née Liu. His father was deceased and his stepmother living. His elder brothers were Li, Xi, Rui (a Participation Adviser), Lian, Lin (a Medical Instructor), and Ying; his younger brother was Lang. His wife was née Yin. He placed forty-third in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hu Jing, registered in a military household in Bin Subprefecture, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Weizhi; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-five sui, born on the twenty-first day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Bogao; his grandfather, Ming, was a Chief Clerk; his father, Yi, held the honorary designation of Official for Righteousness; and his mother was née Wang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Ji, Ji, and Chun, and his wife was née Wang. He placed seventy-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 270th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Shi Zhao, courtesy name Jinghui, was from Binzhou, Ji’nan Prefecture, Shandong, with civilian household registration; a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-seven, and born on the eighteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhongliang, his grandfather Min, his father Jun, and his mother née Zhang; both parents were living, his younger brothers were Song and Yan, and his wife was née Xiao; he placed twenty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 254th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Huai, courtesy name Boyuan, was from Jing County, Ningguo Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, with civilian household registration; a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged forty-three, and born on the twenty-second day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ziren, his grandfather Yongcheng, his father Yuanzhong, and his mother née Wu; both parents were living, his elder brother was Boyi, his younger brothers were Bohou and Boheng, and his wife was née Dong; he placed 132nd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and thirty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jiao Shao, courtesy name Fengyi, was from Guan County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, with civilian household registration; a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was fifth in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Min, Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice, his grandfather Kerang, Administrator, his father Liang, Assistant Instructor, his mother née Wang, and his stepmother née Wu; both parents were living, his elder brothers were Taihe, Zhihe, Menghe, and Yonghe, and his wife was née Yang; he placed forty-ninth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 217th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Ying, courtesy name Shengyuan, was a native of Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, registered as a guardsman of the Embroidered-uniform Guard and enrolled in the Confucian school of Shuntian Prefecture; specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged forty-three, and born on the twenty-seventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Taiqi, a Confucian scholar granted the privilege of wearing official cap and girdle, his grandfather Luo, his father Jin, his mother née Shao, and his stepmothers née Ji and née Wu; both parents were living, his younger brother was Lang, and his wife was née Chen; he placed 135th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Liu Hao, registered in a civilian household in Anfu County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a county school student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Yuanchong; he ranked first in birth order and was thirty-four years old, born on the twelfth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Mingjin, his grandfather Bingji, his father Tingxi, and his mother née Zhao. His grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Yuan, Cheng, Qian, and Run. He married a woman née Huang and subsequently a woman née Ouyang. He placed eightieth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and seventy-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cheng Xu, registered in a civilian household in Shangrao County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Tingchen; he ranked twenty-third in birth order and was forty-two years old, born on the first day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yuanzhe, his grandfather Li𣇠 [second character’s reading uncertain], his father Chun, and his mother née Zheng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Huang and Zhen. He married a woman née Yu and subsequently a woman née Xu. He placed ninety-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and seventy-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Xingming, registered in a military household in Xiao County, Xuzhou, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a county school student specializing in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Chengfu; he ranked first in birth order and was twenty-one years old, born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yan, a commander of ten thousand under the Yuan dynasty; his grandfather was Zhi; his father was Bin, a county magistrate; and his mother was née Ouyang. Both parents were living. He married a woman née Shang. He placed one hundred sixteenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and two hundred ninety-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Ang, registered in a civilian household in Xingan County, Linjiang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was You’ang; he ranked fifth in birth order and was forty-one years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yiqing, his grandfather Yongxuan, his father Yueyin, and his mother née Chen. Both parents were deceased. His younger brothers were Youxian and Youwen. He married a woman née Wang. He placed sixty-seventh in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and two hundred eighty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ren Jizu, registered in Xiangcheng County, Chenzhou, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Shuzhi. Second in birth order, he was aged thirty-four and was born on the tenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jing; his grandfather, Xiu, was a District Magistrate; his father was Cong, and his mother was née Sun. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Jixian; his younger brothers were Zhen, Ang, Bang, Jing, and Chun [name divisions uncertain]. His wife was née Yan. He ranked fourteenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 240th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qian Hao, registered with the Rear Guard of the Nanjing Garrison, belonged to an official household and was a student of the Yingtian Prefectural School. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Jingzong. Fourth in birth order, he was aged forty-four and was born on the second day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhenyi, his grandfather Fuguan, and his father Gui; his mother was née Yang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yong, an honorary official, Pu, and Hong, a Commander; his younger brothers were Han, □ [illegible], and Shu. His wife was née Yan. He ranked seventy-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 213th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Shen, registered in Ye County, Laizhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Peijiao. Third in birth order, he was aged thirty-four and was born on the twentieth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhongxian, his grandfather Feng, and his father Cong, a Registrar; his mother was née Zhao. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Gang and Jing, and his younger brother was Ji. His wife was née Zhou. He ranked fourteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 238th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xing Hong, registered in Dingxiang County, Xinzhou, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Deyu. Third in birth order, he was aged thirty-five and was born on the first day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fengzu, his grandfather An, and his father Ziwen; his mother was née Hu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Guan and Ju, and his younger brothers were Hai and Shen. His wife was née Zhang. He ranked forty-ninth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 213th in the Metropolitan Examination.

汪侃〔貫直隸徽州府歙縣，民籍，國子生，治春秋，字仲和，行二，年三十一，九月二十九日生〕。曾祖嶽寶，祖子義，父仕寧，母徐氏，繼母江氏。具慶下，兄倫，弟任，娶葉氏，繼娶柯氏。應天府鄉試第一百二十七名，會試第一百三十八名。

蔡輔〔貫江西饒州府安仁縣，民籍，國子生，治易經，字咨政，行九，年四十，三月十七日生〕。曾祖伯榮，祖循〔知縣〕，父獻，母周氏。具慶下，弟軒、軾，娶吳氏。江西鄉試第四十六名，會試第九十八名。

張瑞〔貫福建興化府莆田縣，鹽籍，國子生，治詩經，字廷信，行三，年三十五，十一月二十日生〕。曾祖彥肅，祖惟益〔封評事〕，父時復，母陳氏。嚴侍下，兄琦〔義官〕，弟瑛、琇、瑋、璠、琚、璇，娶朱氏。福建鄉試第三十六名，會試第二百九十三名。

屈霖〔貫直隸常州府江陰縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字天澤，行二，年三十六，正月初一日生〕。曾祖原道，祖宗祥，父遂良，母陶氏。慈侍下，兄廷威〔國子生〕，娶顧氏。應天府鄉試第一百三十二名，會試第三十名。
translation_en:
Wang Kan, registered in She County, Huizhou Prefecture, Zhili, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Zhonghe; he ranked second among his brothers, was aged thirty-one, and was born on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Yuebao, his grandfather Ziyi, and his father Shining; his mother was née Xu and his stepmother née Jiang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Lun and his younger brother Ren. He married a woman née Ye and subsequently a woman née Ke. He placed 127th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 138th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cai Fu, registered in Anren County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zizheng; he ranked ninth among his brothers, was aged forty, and was born on the seventeenth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Borong, his grandfather Xun (Magistrate), and his father Xian; his mother was née Zhou. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xuan and Shi. He married a woman née Wu. He placed 46th in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 98th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Rui, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a salt-producing household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Tingxin; he ranked third among his brothers, was aged thirty-five, and was born on the twentieth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Yansu, his grandfather Weiyi (granted the title of Case Reviewer), and his father Shifu; his mother was née Chen. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brother was Qi (an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions); his younger brothers were Ying, Xiu, Wei, Fan, Ju, and Xuan. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed 36th in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 293rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qu Lin, registered in Jiangyin County, Changzhou Prefecture, Zhili, belonged to a civilian household and was a county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Tianze; he ranked second among his brothers, was aged thirty-six, and was born on the first day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Yuandao, his grandfather Zongxiang, and his father Suiliang; his mother was née Tao. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Tingwei (a student of the Imperial University). He married a woman née Gu. He placed 132nd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 30th in the Metropolitan Examination.

曾祖真　祖文質　父英　母關氏

punctuated:
徐瑤〔貫浙江嘉興府嘉興縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字文舟，行二，年二十八，三月十五日生〕。曾祖誠，祖敏，父潮，母沈氏。重慶下，兄瓊，娶宗氏。浙江鄉試第二十三名，會試第五十一名。

呂鵬〔貫四川夔州府達縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字摶萬，行一，年二十九，正月初一日生〕。曾祖亨中〔陰陽訓術〕，祖鎮，父瑭〔監生〕，母高氏。具慶下，弟鵷，娶杜氏。四川鄉試第六十五名，會試第二百四十七名。

熊槩〔貫河南汝寧府光州商城縣，軍籍，國子生，治詩經，字大節，行一，年四十三，三月初一日生〕。曾祖真，祖文質，父英，母闕氏。永感下，弟棨，娶魯氏。河南鄉試第六十三名，會試第二百九十一名。
translation_en:
Xu Yao 徐瑤 was registered in Jiaxing County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Wenzhou; he was second in birth order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the fifteenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Min, his father Chao, and his mother née Shen. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother was Qiong, and he married a woman née Zong. He ranked twenty-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and fifty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lü Peng 呂鵬 was registered in Da County, Kuizhou Prefecture, Sichuan, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Tuanwan; he was first in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the first day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hengzhong, Instructor in the School of Yin and Yang; his grandfather was Zhen; his father was Tang, a student of the Directorate of Education; and his mother was née Gao. Both his parents were living. His younger brother was Yuan, and he married a woman née Du. He ranked sixty-fifth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 247th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiong Gai 熊槩 was registered in Shangcheng County, Guang Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Dajie; he was first in birth order, aged forty-three, and born on the first day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen, his grandfather Wenzhi, his father Ying, and his mother née Que. Both his parents were deceased. His younger brother was Qi, and he married a woman née Lu. He ranked sixty-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 291st in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰自昔帝王
創造丕圖必有貽
謀以為長治久安
之計夏商周之蹟
見于經漢唐宋之
===
事具于史朕欲聞
其紀綱統體制度
得失之詳迨其嗣
世之君欲保盈成
以躋至治一惟舊

translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “Since ancient times, emperors and kings, when founding their great enterprises, invariably left plans for their descendants as a means of securing enduring order and lasting peace. The accomplishments of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou appear in the Classics; the affairs of the Han, Tang, and Song are fully recorded in the histories. I wish to hear in detail about their governing principles and overall organization, and the merits and failings of their institutions. When their successors wished to preserve the prosperity and achievements they had inherited and attain the highest order of government, they looked solely to the old …

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
典是遵是用其或
久也不能無偏而
不舉之處則亦興
其滯補其弊期使
斯民得被先王之
===
澤如夏啓商宗周
宣王是已而漢唐
宋之君亦有能庶
幾者乎朕欲究其
奮勵有為功業可

translation_en: … established statutes were followed and put into practice. If, over time, some matters inevitably became neglected or were left unattended, they revived what had fallen into abeyance and remedied its defects, hoping to enable the people to receive the beneficence of the former kings. Such were Qi of Xia, Zong of Shang [?], and King Xuan of Zhou. Among the rulers of Han, Tang, and Song, were there also any who could approach these examples? I wish to examine their vigorous and purposeful efforts and their achievements that might be …

text:

徒泛論古之人而
不求今時之急務
亦非納言之善也

translation_en:
…the substance of their achievements worthy of praise. Without examining antiquity, there is indeed no basis for assessing the present. Yet merely discussing men of antiquity in general terms, without investigating the urgent tasks of our own time, is likewise no sound way of offering counsel.
Formerly, Our Emperor Taizu Gao unified all under Heaven, establishing institutions and bequeathing standards to be revered for ten thousand generations. Emperor Taizong Wen established the seat of imperial rule in the two…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
京洪謨遠略光前
裕後
列聖相承益隆繼述
斯民樂育於熙皡
之治已百二十年
===
矣然治極而弛理
勢自然
祖宗良法美意豈能
悉祗承而無弊乎
肆朕惓惓以法
alt_text:
京洪謨遠略光前
裕後
列聖相承益隆繼述
斯民樂育於熙皡
之治已百二十年
矣然治極而弛理
勢自然
===
祖宗良法美意豈能
恙祇峯而無弊乎
肆朕惓惓以法
punctuated: 京，洪謨遠略，光前裕後。列聖相承，益隆繼述，斯民樂育於熙皡之治，已百二十年矣。然治極而弛，理勢自然。祖宗良法美意，豈能悉祗承而無弊乎？肆朕惓惓以法
translation_en: …capitals. His grand plans and far-reaching strategies brought glory to his predecessors and abundance to posterity. Successive sage emperors inherited the throne, ever furthering the work of their predecessors. The people have flourished happily under this radiant and harmonious rule for a hundred and twenty years. Yet when government reaches its height, laxity follows: this is the natural course of things. Could the excellent laws and fine intentions of Our ancestors all have been reverently upheld without abuses arising? Thus We are earnestly intent upon emulating…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
祖為念欲俾内外百
司羣工庶職咸思
奮庸熈載恪守
典訓而慎行之毋滋
偏失不舉名存實
===
爽之譏用期吏稱
其職民安其業中
國尊而四夷服風
雨時而嘉祥至諒
必有道矣爾諸生
alt_text:
祖為念欲俾內外百
司羣工庶職咸思
奮庸熙載恪守
典訓而慎行之毋滋
偏失不舉名存實
===
爽之議用期吏稱
其職民安其業中
國尊而四夷賓服風
雨時而嘉祥至諒
必有道矣爾諸生
punctuated: 祖為念，欲俾内外百司羣工庶職咸思奮庸熈載，恪守典訓而慎行之，毋滋偏失不舉、名存實爽之譏。用期吏稱其職，民安其業，中國尊而四夷服，風雨時而嘉祥至，諒必有道矣。爾諸生
translation_en: …with emulating My ancestors as My concern, I wish to make all offices and officials, within the capital and beyond, in every post, resolve to exert themselves in service and bring their work to fruition, reverently uphold the established teachings, and carefully put them into practice, without inviting criticism for deviations and failures to act, or for preserving the name while betraying the substance. Thus I hope that officials will fulfill their duties, the people will pursue their livelihoods in peace, the Central Kingdom will be honored and the peoples of the four quarters will submit, winds and rains will come in season, and auspicious signs will appear. Surely there must be a way to achieve this. You students…

…all have studied antiquity, mastered the Classics, and aspire to serve the world. Let each of you respond frankly, concealing nothing. I shall personally read your answers.

The fifteenth day of the third month of the twenty-third year of Chenghua (1487).

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
臣費宏
臣對臣聞帝王之御天下也有致治之道有保
治之道致治之道存乎法保治之道存乎勤非
法無以維天下之勢非勤無以守天下之法故
創造丕圖者必立法以貽孫謀嗣守鴻圖者必
憂勤以繩祖武曰紀綱曰統體曰制度皆法之
具也而興滯補弊則勤之實耳創之者以法則
國勢尊嚴而有以成長治之業守之者以勤則
法度脩舉而有以躋至治之休帝王御天下之
道夫豈有外於此乎夏商周之治所以卓冠千
===
古以其創之者其法善而守之者其志勤也漢
唐宋之治不古若庸非創之者其法有未善守
之者其勤有未至歟恭惟
皇帝陛下年當鼎盛運撫盈成昧爽臨朝惟
祖宗之法是遵甲夜視事惟
祖宗之法是監
臨御以來于兹二紀賢才皆已舉用四海皆已無
虞保治之道盖已默得于
聖心之妙矣尤不自足乃於
萬幾之暇

臣對：臣聞帝王之御天下也，有致治之道，有保治之道。致治之道存乎法，保治之道存乎勤。非法無以維天下之勢，非勤無以守天下之法。故創造丕圖者，必立法以貽孫謀；嗣守鴻圖者，必憂勤以繩祖武。曰紀綱，曰統體，曰制度，皆法之具也；而興滯補弊，則勤之實耳。創之者以法，則國勢尊嚴，而有以成長治之業；守之者以勤，則法度脩舉，而有以躋至治之休。帝王御天下之道，夫豈有外於此乎？夏商周之治所以卓冠千古，以其創之者其法善，而守之者其志勤也。漢唐宋之治不古若，庸非創之者其法有未善，守之者其勤有未至歟？
恭惟皇帝陛下，年當鼎盛，運撫盈成。昧爽臨朝，惟祖宗之法是遵；甲夜視事，惟祖宗之法是監。臨御以來，于兹二紀，賢才皆已舉用，四海皆已無虞。保治之道，盖已默得于聖心之妙矣。尤不自足，乃於萬幾之暇
translation_en:
Your servant, Fei Hong.
Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings govern All under Heaven, there is a way to establish good order and a way to preserve it. The way to establish good order lies in laws and institutions; the way to preserve it lies in diligence. Without laws and institutions, there is no means to sustain the realm’s strength; without diligence, there is no means to uphold its laws and institutions. Thus, those who found a great imperial enterprise must establish laws to leave as a plan for their descendants; those who inherit and preserve that enterprise must exercise vigilant diligence to follow in their ancestors’ footsteps. Guiding principles, the overall structure of government, and institutional arrangements are all instruments of law; reviving what has fallen into neglect and remedying defects are the substance of diligence. If founders act through laws and institutions, the state’s authority will command respect, enabling them to establish enduring order. If successors preserve it through diligence, laws and standards will be maintained and put into effect, enabling them to attain the blessings of consummate government. Can the way in which emperors and kings govern All under Heaven lie anywhere beyond this? The government of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou stood preeminent throughout the ages because their founders’ laws were good and their successors were committed to diligence. The government of the Han, Tang, and Song fell short of antiquity: was this not because their founders’ laws were imperfect and their successors’ diligence insufficient?
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor is in the prime of life and presides over an era of full accomplishment. At dawn you attend court, following only the laws of your imperial ancestors; during the first watch of the night you attend to affairs, taking only their laws as your guide. In the twenty-four years since you assumed the throne, worthy and talented men have all been selected and employed, and all within the Four Seas has become free from anxiety. Surely, through the subtle wisdom of your sagely mind, you have already inwardly grasped the way to preserve good order. Yet you remain unsatisfied with your own achievements, and so, in moments of respite from the myriad affairs of state…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
廷集多士諮諏治道首舉三代漢唐宋之創業着
而欲聞其紀綱統體制度得失之詳中舉三代
漢唐宋之守成者而欲究其奮勵有為功業可
稱之實末復以
祖宗列聖之所以創守為言而慮夫成法之弊且惓
惓以法
祖為念期于吏稱民安中國尊而四夷服風雨時而
嘉祥至臣伏而讀之有以見
陛下知創業之惟艱念守成之不易而欲保熙皥之
治於無窮也臣請稽之經訂之史按之當今之
===
務為
陛下陳之
陛下幸垂聽焉臣聞天下重器也創之至艱守之至
艱創之而不知所以創之之道則無以垂治於
百王守之而不知所以守之之道則無以保治
於萬世創之之道無他焉臣前所謂法是已守
之之道無他焉臣前所謂勤是已盖法者維持
天下之具故帝王創業必建立紀綱經畫統體
條陳制度以畫天下之法以貽子孫之謀以為
長治久安之計自家而國自國而天下彼此相

廷集多士，諮諏治道。首舉三代漢唐宋之創業着，而欲聞其紀綱統體制度得失之詳；中舉三代漢唐宋之守成者，而欲究其奮勵有為、功業可稱之實；末復以祖宗列聖之所以創守為言，而慮夫成法之弊，且惓惓以法祖為念，期于吏稱民安，中國尊而四夷服，風雨時而嘉祥至。臣伏而讀之，有以見陛下知創業之惟艱，念守成之不易，而欲保熙皥之治於無窮也。臣請稽之經，訂之史，按之當今之務，為陛下陳之。陛下幸垂聽焉。

臣聞天下重器也，創之至艱，守之至艱。創之而不知所以創之之道，則無以垂治於百王；守之而不知所以守之之道，則無以保治於萬世。創之之道無他焉，臣前所謂法是已；守之之道無他焉，臣前所謂勤是已。盖法者，維持天下之具。故帝王創業，必建立紀綱，經畫統體，條陳制度，以畫天下之法，以貽子孫之謀，以為長治久安之計。自家而國，自國而天下，彼此相
translation_en:
…you assembled the many scholars at court and consulted them on the Way of government. First, you cited the founders of the Three Dynasties, Han, Tang, and Song, wishing to hear in detail about the strengths and shortcomings of their governing principles, overall organization, and institutions. Next, you cited those who preserved the achievements of the Three Dynasties, Han, Tang, and Song, wishing to investigate the actual substance of their vigorous endeavors and praiseworthy accomplishments. Finally, you spoke of how your ancestors, the successive sage emperors, founded and preserved the dynasty, expressing concern about defects in established institutions. With unflagging devotion, you have kept emulating your ancestors foremost in mind, hoping that officials will fulfill their duties and the people live in peace, that the Central Kingdom will be honored and the peoples of the four quarters submit, and that wind and rain will come in season and auspicious signs appear. Your servant has read this with reverence and perceives that Your Majesty understands the difficulty of founding a dynasty, reflects upon the difficulty of preserving its achievements, and wishes to maintain bright and harmonious government forever. I beg leave to examine the Classics, verify their teachings against the histories, and assess them in light of present affairs, so that I may set these matters before Your Majesty. May Your Majesty graciously give ear.

Your servant has heard that All-under-Heaven is a weighty vessel: to establish rule over it is exceedingly difficult, and to preserve that rule is exceedingly difficult. If one establishes it without understanding the Way by which it is established, one cannot bequeath good government to a hundred succeeding kings. If one preserves it without understanding the Way by which it is preserved, one cannot maintain good government for ten thousand generations. The Way of establishing it is nothing other than what your servant earlier called institutions; the Way of preserving it is nothing other than what your servant earlier called diligence. Institutions are the means by which All-under-Heaven is sustained. Thus, when emperors and kings found their rule, they must establish governing principles, plan the overall organization, and set out institutional arrangements in detail, thereby laying down rules for All-under-Heaven, bequeathing plans to their descendants, and providing for lasting order and enduring peace. From the family to the state, and from the state to All-under-Heaven, each mutually …

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
維內外相制如身之使臂臂之使指者紀綱之
謂也或尚寬大或尚嚴明以此而始以此而終
不朝文而暮質以自潰亂者統體之謂也治教
禮樂田賦兵刑之類所以經緯天地黼黻民物
者制度之謂也然先王之法必有偏而不起之
處故政有眊而不行守成者欲保盈成以躋至
治又必勤勵不息興其滯以補其弊然後天下
之法可以施諸罔極先王之澤可以波及斯民
而世為有道之國矣臣請以創之之法言之禹
之造夏有典則以貽子孫觀其文命四敷聲教
四訖則有以立乎紀綱政尚忠朴治先勤儉則
有以定乎統體至於建官二百肉辟三千設六
師以討罪辨三壤以成賦天秩有禮大夏有樂
教民以序正朔以寅其制度又無不備禹之立
法貽謀其善如此夏之治安於此乎致矣湯之
造商昭大德以裕後昆觀其肇脩人紀而九有
有截則紀綱以立代虐以寬而兆民允懷則統
體以定至於建二相以摠百官制官刑以儆有
位公田藉而不稅大輅質而得中國老養於右
學庶老養於左學其制度亦無不備湯之立法

學庶老養於左學其制度亦無不備湯之立法
punctuated:
維，內外相制，如身之使臂、臂之使指者，紀綱之謂也。或尚寬大，或尚嚴明，以此而始，以此而終，不朝文而暮質以自潰亂者，統體之謂也。治教禮樂、田賦兵刑之類，所以經緯天地、黼黻民物者，制度之謂也。然先王之法，必有偏而不起之處，故政有眊而不行。守成者欲保盈成，以躋至治，又必勤勵不息，興其滯以補其弊。然後天下之法可以施諸罔極，先王之澤可以波及斯民，而世為有道之國矣。
臣請以創之之法言之。禹之造夏，有典則以貽子孫。觀其文命四敷，聲教四訖，則有以立乎紀綱；政尚忠朴，治先勤儉，則有以定乎統體。至於建官二百，肉辟三千，設六師以討罪，辨三壤以成賦，天秩有禮，大夏有樂，教民以序，正朔以寅，其制度又無不備。禹之立法貽謀，其善如此，夏之治安於此乎致矣。
湯之造商，昭大德以裕後昆。觀其肇脩人紀，而九有有截，則紀綱以立；代虐以寬，而兆民允懷，則統體以定。至於建二相以摠百官，制官刑以儆有位，公田藉而不稅，大輅質而得中，國老養於右學，庶老養於左學，其制度亦無不備。湯之立法
translation_en:
…held together, with the inner and outer spheres checking one another, like the body directing the arms and the arms directing the fingers: this is what is meant by the guiding principles of government. To esteem either magnanimity or strict clarity, to begin and end by the same principle, and not to favor refinement in the morning and simplicity in the evening, thereby bringing disorder and collapse upon oneself: this is what is meant by the overall framework of rule. Administration and education, rites and music, land and taxation, military affairs and punishments—these are the means of ordering Heaven and Earth and embellishing the lives of the people and all things: this is what is meant by institutions. Yet the laws of former kings inevitably contain points that are unbalanced and cannot be put into effect [?]; thus some measures become obscure and fail to operate. Those who preserve an established realm, wishing to safeguard its fullness and achievement and attain the highest order, must also exert themselves tirelessly, revive what has stagnated, and remedy its defects. Only then can the laws of the realm be applied without limit, the beneficence of former kings reach these people, and the state remain governed according to the Way from generation to generation.
Your servant asks leave to discuss the laws by which dynasties were founded. When Yu founded the Xia, he had statutes and standards to bequeath to his descendants. Consider how his civilizing influence spread in all directions and his renown and teaching reached every quarter: thereby he established the guiding principles of government. His administration esteemed sincerity and simplicity, and his rule gave priority to diligence and frugality: thereby he settled the overall framework of rule. As for establishing two hundred offices, providing three thousand provisions for corporal punishment, organizing the Six Armies to punish the guilty, and distinguishing three classes of soil to determine taxation; providing rites that embodied Heaven’s ordering and music in the Great Xia dance; teaching the people through local schools and setting the first month of the year in the month designated yin—his institutions were complete in every respect. Such was the excellence of Yu’s establishment of laws and provision of plans for posterity. Through these the Xia attained good order and peace.
When Tang founded the Shang, he manifested great virtue to enrich the legacy of his descendants. Consider how he first set human relationships in order, so that the Nine Regions were uniformly governed: thereby the guiding principles of government were established. He replaced tyranny with magnanimity, and the myriad people sincerely cherished him: thereby the overall framework of rule was settled. As for establishing two chief ministers to direct all officials, instituting punishments for officials to admonish those holding office, requiring collective labor on public fields instead of levying a tax, making the great state carriage plain yet fitting, supporting the elders of the state in the Right School and elderly commoners in the Left School—his institutions too were complete in every respect. Tang’s establishment of laws…

貽謀其善如此商之治安於此乎致矣若夫周
之文武啓佑後人咸正罔缺風化基於關雎內
庭屬於冢宰樞機周密有以為四方之綱明德
而不敢忽慎罰而不敢濫仁愛忠厚有以為一
代之體其建官也六卿分職其制刑也三典詰
姦田賦有鄉遂都鄙之殊軍賦有鄉遂丘甸之
異語禮樂則五禮以節民性六樂以和民聲語
教化則三物以興賢能四術以造俊秀制度之
盛又何如也周之治安何莫而不本於立法貽
謀之善乎下逮漢唐宋創業之君非不欲致治

苛以寬仁為統體命蕭何次律令命叔孫通制
禮儀章程定於張蒼軍法申於韓信所以貽謀

之非大體雖寬而卒不能除參夷之令庶事草

punctuated:
貽謀，其善如此，商之治安於此乎致矣。若夫周之文武，啓佑後人，咸正罔缺，風化基於關雎，內庭屬於冢宰，樞機周密，有以為四方之綱；明德而不敢忽，慎罰而不敢濫，仁愛忠厚，有以為一代之體。其建官也，六卿分職；其制刑也，三典詰姦。田賦有鄉遂都鄙之殊，軍賦有鄉遂丘甸之異。語禮樂，則五禮以節民性，六樂以和民聲；語教化，則三物以興賢能，四術以造俊秀。制度之盛又何如也！周之治安，何莫而不本於立法貽謀之善乎？下逮漢唐宋，創業之君非不欲致治如三代也，但其法有未善耳。
漢之高帝，大封同姓，委任大臣，以規模為紀綱；約法順民，掃除煩苛，以寬仁為統體。命蕭何次律令，命叔孫通制禮儀，章程定於張蒼，軍法申於韓信，所以貽謀者又有制度矣。然大綱雖正，而終不能無雜伯之非；大體雖寬，而卒不能除參夷之令。庶事草創，而井田不復，學校不興；禮文多闕，而正朔不改，官名不定，則其法不能以皆善也。
唐之太宗，除亂致治，四夷賓服，庶乎知立國之紀綱；屈己從諫，仁心愛人，庶乎知為政之統體。以職事任
translation_en:
…such was the excellence of his provision of plans for posterity; through this the Shang attained good government and peace. As for Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou, they guided and aided their successors, putting everything right without omission. Their moral influence was founded on “Guanju” (“The Ospreys”), and the inner court was placed under the Minister of State. The central organs of government were closely coordinated, providing a guiding framework for the four quarters. They made virtue manifest without daring to be negligent, and exercised care in punishment without daring to use it excessively. Benevolence, affection, loyalty, and generosity provided the governing principles for the dynasty. In establishing offices, they divided duties among the six ministers; in instituting punishments, they used the three penal codes to deal with wrongdoing. Land levies differed among the xiang and sui districts and the du and bi domains; military levies differed among the xiang and sui districts and the qiu and dian units. As for rites and music, the five categories of rites regulated the people's dispositions, and the six musical traditions harmonized their voices. As for moral instruction, the three subjects of instruction advanced the worthy and capable, and the four arts cultivated outstanding talent. How splendid their institutions were! What aspect of Zhou's good government and peace did not rest upon the excellence of its laws and its plans for posterity? Coming down to the Han, Tang, and Song, their founding rulers certainly wished to achieve government like that of the Three Dynasties; it was simply that their laws were not wholly good.
Emperor Gao of Han extensively enfeoffed members of his own surname and entrusted great ministers with responsibility, making these broad arrangements his guiding framework. He simplified the laws to accord with the people's wishes and swept away burdensome and harsh measures, making leniency and benevolence his governing principles. He ordered Xiao He to compile the statutes and ordinances, and Shusun Tong to establish ceremonial observances. Zhang Cang settled the regulations, and Han Xin promulgated military law. Thus, his provision for posterity also included established institutions. Yet although his general framework was sound, it could never escape the fault of mixing in the methods of hegemons. Although his overall approach was lenient, he ultimately failed to abolish the ordinance for exterminating the three sets of kin. Affairs were still at an initial stage: the well-field system was not restored, and schools were not established. Ritual forms had many deficiencies: the calendar was not changed, and official titles were not settled. His laws, therefore, could not all be good.
Emperor Taizong of Tang eliminated disorder and achieved good government, and the peoples of the four quarters submitted to him. He came close to understanding the guiding framework for establishing a state. He humbled himself and accepted remonstrance, showing benevolence and love for others. He came close to understanding the governing principles of administration. On the basis of official duties, he appointed…

text:
官以尊本任衆以租庸任民以府衛任兵禮制
於房玄齡樂作於祖孝孫六學有領五刑有覆
所以貽謀者又有制度矣然内多慚德有夷狄
之風漸不克終來諍臣之疏法度之行禮樂之
具擬之先王未備田疇之制庠序之教擬之先
王未詳則其法不能以皆善也至若宋之太祖
以忠厚廉耻為紀綱而五事之美千古所無以
偃兵息民為統體而五季之弊一朝頓解兩府
臺諫官之總察有方三衙四廂兵之簡閱有道
幸學有賛均田有令而教養之法可觀溫叟制
===
禮和峴制樂而禮樂之文可取又有制度以貽
謀矣然宗室則無選舉教訓之實宿衛則聚卒
伍無賴之人官司之課試不嚴學校之作成無
要兵士毎雜於疲老農民常苦於征繇其法又
豈能盡善哉由是觀之則
聖策所謂紀綱統體制度得失之詳可得而知矣臣
請以守之之勤言之夏當有扈違命之時三正

官，以尊本任衆，以租庸任民，以府衛任兵。禮制於房玄齡，樂作於祖孝孫，六學有領，五刑有覆，所以貽謀者又有制度矣。然内多慚德，有夷狄之風；漸不克終，來諍臣之疏。法度之行、禮樂之具，擬之先王未備；田疇之制、庠序之教，擬之先王未詳，則其法不能以皆善也。至若宋之太祖，以忠厚廉耻為紀綱，而五事之美，千古所無；以偃兵息民為統體，而五季之弊，一朝頓解。兩府臺諫，官之總察有方；三衙四廂，兵之簡閱有道。幸學有賛，均田有令，而教養之法可觀；溫叟制禮，和峴制樂，而禮樂之文可取，又有制度以貽謀矣。然宗室則無選舉教訓之實，宿衛則聚卒伍無賴之人；官司之課試不嚴，學校之作成無要；兵士毎雜於疲老，農民常苦於征繇，其法又豈能盡善哉？由是觀之，則聖策所謂紀綱、統體、制度得失之詳，可得而知矣。

…officials; he assigned responsibilities to the populace by honoring the fundamental occupation of agriculture [?], to the common people through grain taxes and labor-service commutation, and to soldiers through the military garrisons and guards. Fang Xuanling established ritual, and Zu Xiaosun composed music. The six schools had supervision, and sentences under the five punishments underwent review. Thus, the plans he bequeathed to posterity also included institutions and regulations. Yet within his household there was much shameful conduct, displaying the customs of the Yi and Di peoples. Gradually he failed to sustain his initial efforts, prompting memorials from remonstrating ministers. The implementation of laws and the provision of rites and music were incomplete when measured against the former kings; the arrangements for farmland and instruction in schools were insufficiently developed by the same measure. Thus, his laws could not all be good.
As for Emperor Taizu of the Song, he made loyalty, generosity, integrity, and a sense of shame his guiding principles: the excellence of his five deeds was unparalleled through the ages. He made laying down arms and giving the people respite his overarching framework, and the evils of the Five Dynasties were suddenly dispelled in a single morning. Through the two chief councils, the Censorate, and the remonstrance officials, he had sound means of comprehensively overseeing officials; through the three military commands and four divisions, he had proper methods for selecting and reviewing troops. His visits to the schools received eulogies, and he issued orders to equalize landholding: his methods of educating and sustaining the people were worthy of admiration. Wensou established ritual, and He Xian established music: their ritual and musical forms were worthy of adoption. Here too were institutions and regulations bequeathed to posterity. Yet there was no substantive selection, advancement, education, or discipline of the imperial clansmen, while the palace guard gathered disreputable men from the ranks. Assessments of officials were not rigorous, and the schools lacked effective means of developing talent. The soldiers frequently included the infirm and aged, and farmers constantly suffered from levies and labor service. How, then, could his laws have been wholly good? Viewed in this light, the particulars of the merits and failings of guiding principles, overarching frameworks, and institutions and regulations, mentioned in Your Majesty’s policy question, can be understood.

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
先王之澤而謳歌有歸有夏盈成之治以勤而
保矣商自盤庚既沒之後賞刑僭濫荊楚叛背
湯之法不能無偏而不起之處也高宗則監于
先王成憲而奮曰勵有為興滯補弊求良弼以代
王言裒荊旅以昭殷武卒使民被先王之澤而
小大無怨有商盈成之治以勤而保矣至若周
自厲王之烈小雅盡廢而四夷交侵上帝板蕩
而下民卒癉文武之法不能無偏而不起之處
矣宣王由是奮勵有為興衰撥亂車攻復古明
文武之功業六月出師復文武之境土卒使王
===
化大行流離還定周之盈成何莫而不保於興
滯補弊之勤乎下逮漢唐宋守成之君非不欲
保治如三代也但其勤有未至耳漢之宣帝光
武庶幾法祖之君也或承武昭虛耗之弊而綜
核名實信賞必罰伸威北狄功光祖宗或鑒西
京不競之禍而明慎政體揔攬權綱身致太平
恢復前烈其興滯補弊之功業有可稱者惜夫
神爵之後頗尚荒唐建武之中竟行封禪則其
勤有未至焉唐之玄宗憲宗庶幾法祖之君也
或革前朝權戚之弊而勵精政事開元之際幾

先王之澤，而謳歌有歸，有夏盈成之治以勤而保矣。商自盤庚既沒之後，賞刑僭濫，荊楚叛背，湯之法不能無偏而不起之處也。高宗則監于先王成憲，而奮曰勵有為，興滯補弊，求良弼以代王言，裒荊旅以昭殷武，卒使民被先王之澤，而小大無怨，有商盈成之治以勤而保矣。至若周，自厲王之烈，小雅盡廢，而四夷交侵，上帝板蕩，而下民卒癉，文武之法不能無偏而不起之處矣。宣王由是奮勵有為，興衰撥亂，《車攻》復古，明文武之功業；《六月》出師，復文武之境土。卒使王化大行，流離還定，周之盈成何莫而不保於興滯補弊之勤乎？
下逮漢唐宋，守成之君非不欲保治如三代也，但其勤有未至耳。漢之宣帝、光武，庶幾法祖之君也。或承武昭虛耗之弊，而綜核名實，信賞必罰，伸威北狄，功光祖宗；或鑒西京不競之禍，而明慎政體，揔攬權綱，身致太平，恢復前烈。其興滯補弊之功業有可稱者。惜夫神爵之後，頗尚荒唐；建武之中，竟行封禪，則其勤有未至焉。唐之玄宗、憲宗，庶幾法祖之君也。或革前朝權戚之弊，而勵精政事，開元之際，幾
translation_en:
…the beneficence of the former kings, and their songs of praise found their rightful recipient. Thus the flourishing order of the Xia was preserved through diligence. In the Shang, after Pan Geng’s death, rewards and punishments became arbitrary and excessive, and Jing and Chu rebelled. Tang’s institutions inevitably had aspects that had become distorted and fallen into disuse. Gaozong took the established statutes of the former kings as his model and energetically applied himself to action [?], reviving what had languished and remedying abuses. He sought a worthy adviser to speak on the king’s behalf and mustered forces against Jing to display the martial might of the Yin. Ultimately, he enabled the people to enjoy the beneficence of the former kings, so that neither great nor small harbored resentment. Thus the flourishing order of the Shang was preserved through diligence. As for the Zhou, following King Li’s tyranny, the principles celebrated in the Lesser Odes were wholly abandoned, and the peoples of the four quarters invaded from every side. Heaven brought disorder and upheaval, and the common people were all afflicted. The institutions of Kings Wen and Wu inevitably had aspects that had become distorted and fallen into disuse. King Xuan therefore applied himself vigorously to action, reversing decline and restoring order. As celebrated in “The Chariots Attack” (Che gong), he restored ancient practices and made manifest the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu; as celebrated in “The Sixth Month” (Liu yue), he dispatched troops and recovered their territories. Ultimately, kingly moral influence spread far and wide, and those who had been displaced returned to settled lives. Was not every aspect of Zhou’s flourishing order preserved through diligent efforts to revive what had languished and remedy abuses?
Coming down to the Han, Tang, and Song, rulers who inherited an established order were not without the desire to preserve good government as the Three Dynasties had done. It was simply that their diligence fell short. Emperors Xuandi and Guangwu of the Han came close to being rulers who modeled themselves on their ancestors. The former inherited the depletion and exhaustion left by Emperors Wudi and Zhaodi, scrutinized actual performance against professed responsibilities, made rewards trustworthy and punishments certain, and extended his might over the northern Di, bringing glory to his ancestors through his achievements. The latter took warning from the calamity caused by the weakness of the Western Han court, administered government with discernment and care, held the reins of authority firmly in his own hands, personally brought about peace, and restored the achievements of his predecessors. Their accomplishments in reviving what had languished and remedying abuses deserve praise. Regrettably, after the Shenjue era, Xuandi became rather given to extravagant fantasies; and during the Jianwu era, Guangwu went so far as to perform the feng and shan sacrifices to Heaven and Earth. In these respects their diligence fell short. Emperors Xuanzong and Xianzong of the Tang likewise came close to being rulers who modeled themselves on their ancestors. The former eliminated the abuses of powerful imperial relatives from the preceding reigns and devoted himself energetically to government; during the Kaiyuan era, he almost…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
致太平或懲德宗姑息之禍而紀律畢張元和
之初威令復振其興滯補弊之功業有可稱者
惜夫天寶之末嗜慾滋生平蔡之後侈心遽動
則其勤有未至焉至若宋仁宗承宮闈專政之
後裁抑僥倖銳意太平神宗當累朝委靡之餘
勤儉有為勵精求治亦可謂善法祖宗而興滯
補弊之功業有足稱者惜夫一則仁柔有餘而
剛斷不足一則聽言太廣而進人太銳其勤又
豈能至哉由是觀之則
聖策所謂奮勵有為功業可稱之實可得而知矣大
===
抵三代之法盡善盡美故其子孫有所據依而
為治也易至於政弊然後變其小節而其大體
卒不可易漢唐宋之法不過因陋就簡以苟一
時之近功其善者常寡而不善者常多其善者
常小而不善者常大立之未幾而弊已隨之後
世之君區區脩補百孔千瘡隨亂隨失雖欲言
治皆苟而已洪惟我
太祖高皇帝混一區宇建制垂憲而法之貽于後者
至精而至備
太宗文皇帝定鼎兩京訏謨定命而法之光于前者
alt_text:
致太平武懲德宗姑息之禍而紀律畢張憲宗
之初威令復振其興滯補弊之功業有可稱者
惜夫天寶之末嗜慾滋生平蔡之後侈心遽動
則其勤有未至焉至若宋仁宗承宮闈專政之
後裁抑僥倖銳意太平神宗當累朝委靡之餘

補弊之功業有足稱者惜夫一則仁柔有餘而
剛斷不足一則聽言太廣而進人太銳其勤又
豈能至哉由是觀之則
聖策所謂奮勵有爲功業可稱之實可得而知矣大
===
抵三代之法盡善盡美故其子孫有所據依而
爲治也易至於政弊然後變其小節而其大體
卒不可易漢唐宋之法不過因陋就簡以苟一
時之近功其善者常寡而不善者常多其善者
常小而不善者常大立之未幾而弊已隨之後
世之君區區脩補百孔千瘡隨亂隨失雖欲言
治皆苟而已洪惟我
太祖高皇帝混一區宇建制垂憲而法之貽于後者
至精而至備
太宗文皇帝定鼎兩京訏謨定命而法之光于前者
punctuated:
致太平；或懲德宗姑息之禍，而紀律畢張，元和之初，威令復振。其興滯補弊之功業有可稱者，惜夫天寶之末，嗜慾滋生；平蔡之後，侈心遽動，則其勤有未至焉。至若宋仁宗承宮闈專政之後，裁抑僥倖，銳意太平；神宗當累朝委靡之餘，勤儉有為，勵精求治，亦可謂善法祖宗，而興滯補弊之功業有足稱者。惜夫一則仁柔有餘而剛斷不足，一則聽言太廣而進人太銳，其勤又豈能至哉？由是觀之，則聖策所謂奮勵有為、功業可稱之實，可得而知矣。
大抵三代之法盡善盡美，故其子孫有所據依，而為治也易。至於政弊，然後變其小節，而其大體卒不可易。漢唐宋之法，不過因陋就簡，以苟一時之近功。其善者常寡，而不善者常多；其善者常小，而不善者常大。立之未幾，而弊已隨之。後世之君區區脩補，百孔千瘡，隨亂隨失，雖欲言治，皆苟而已。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝混一區宇，建制垂憲，而法之貽于後者至精而至備。太宗文皇帝定鼎兩京，訏謨定命，而法之光于前者
translation_en:
…brought about great peace; the other, taking warning from the calamities caused by Dezong’s indulgence, fully established discipline and order, so that at the beginning of the Yuanhe era imperial authority and commands regained their force. Their achievements in reviving what had languished and remedying abuses deserve praise. Regrettably, toward the end of the Tianbao era, appetites and desires multiplied; after the pacification of Cai, a taste for extravagance suddenly arose. Thus their diligence fell short.
As for Renzong of the Song, following a period when the palace quarters monopolized power, he curbed those seeking unmerited favors and devoted himself resolutely to great peace. Shenzong, inheriting the enfeeblement of successive reigns, was diligent, frugal, and active, exerting himself in pursuit of good government. They too may be said to have followed their ancestors well, and their achievements in reviving what had languished and remedying abuses deserve praise. Regrettably, the one had an excess of benevolent gentleness but insufficient firmness and decisiveness; the other listened too indiscriminately to advice and advanced men too hastily. How, then, could their diligence have been complete? Viewed in this light, the actual accomplishments described in Your Majesty’s policy question as energetic endeavor and praiseworthy achievement can be understood.
Generally speaking, the institutions of the Three Dynasties were supremely good and complete. Their descendants therefore had something to rely upon, and governing was easy. Only when abuses arose in administration did they alter minor details; the overall framework ultimately could not be changed. The institutions of the Han, Tang, and Song merely made do with crude and simple arrangements to secure immediate gains for the moment. Their good features were invariably few, their bad features many; their good features were invariably minor, their bad features major. Scarcely had they been established when abuses followed. Later rulers busied themselves with petty repairs to arrangements riddled with holes and wounds, only to encounter disorder and failure at every turn. Though they wished to speak of good government, all they achieved was expediency.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao unified the realm, established institutions, and handed down enduring standards; the laws he bequeathed to posterity were supremely refined and comprehensive. Emperor Taizong Wen established the seats of sovereignty in the two capitals and, through grand designs, secured the dynastic mandate; the laws through which he added luster to his predecessor’s legacy…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
愈盛而愈彰請舉其大者言之
宫闈雍肅而無出梱之言左右忠勤而謹戴盆之
戒任府部為股肱而事權不紊倚臺諫為耳目
而國論有歸
宗子分封以廣維城之助三司並置以革藩鎮之
專申明典常而有以正天下之大誼誅逐胡虜
而有以嚴天下之大防則紀綱之善無異乎三
代矣治本人情而廣孝弟之化仁同一視而無
南北之殊施猛政以濟寬用重典以平亂惠鮮
鰥寡貪墨之加害者必懲懷保小民豪強之凌
===

愈盛而愈彰。請舉其大者言之：宫闈雍肅，而無出梱之言；左右忠勤，而謹戴盆之戒；任府部為股肱，而事權不紊；倚臺諫為耳目，而國論有歸。宗子分封，以廣維城之助；三司並置，以革藩鎮之專；申明典常，而有以正天下之大誼；誅逐胡虜，而有以嚴天下之大防，則紀綱之善無異乎三代矣。治本人情，而廣孝弟之化；仁同一視，而無南北之殊；施猛政以濟寬，用重典以平亂；惠鮮鰥寡，貪墨之加害者必懲；懷保小民，豪強之凌暴者不貸，則統體之善無異乎三代矣。至若審官，立銓選考課之方；育材，設學校科目之典；財以足國，而賦稅漕運有其經；兵以衞民，而番上分屯有其備；禮儀有式，宴享有章，而和敬之風以著；令教於先，律齊於後，而欽恤之意攸存，則制度之善又無異乎三代矣。

translation_en:
…became ever more flourishing and illustrious. Allow me to describe the principal examples. The palace quarters were harmonious and solemn, and no words passed beyond their threshold. The attendants were loyal and diligent, carefully observing the admonition about wearing a basin on one’s head [which prevents one from seeing Heaven]. The commissions and ministries served as arms and legs, with no confusion in their responsibilities and authority; the censorial and remonstrance officials served as eyes and ears, giving deliberations on affairs of state a guiding authority. Princes of the imperial lineage were granted fiefs, extending their support as a protective wall; the three provincial commissions were established side by side, eliminating the exclusive power of regional military governors. Established norms were clarified, rectifying the great moral obligations of the realm; the northern foes were punished and driven out, enforcing the realm’s great boundary between Chinese and barbarians. Thus, the excellence of the governing framework was no different from that of the Three Dynasties.
Government was rooted in human feelings, spreading the transforming influence of filial piety and brotherly respect. Benevolence regarded all alike, making no distinction between north and south. Stern measures complemented leniency, and severe laws quelled disorder. Widowers and widows were shown kindness and enabled to thrive, and corrupt officials who harmed them were invariably punished. The common people were cherished and protected, and powerful men who oppressed them were never pardoned. Thus, the excellence of governance as a whole was no different from that of the Three Dynasties.
As for scrutinizing officials, procedures were established for selection and performance evaluation; for nurturing talent, regulations were instituted for schools and the examination system. Finances supplied the state’s needs, with regular arrangements for taxation and grain transport. Troops protected the people, with provision for rotational service and deployment in separate garrisons. Ritual observances had prescribed forms, and banquets and offerings had established rules, making manifest a spirit of harmony and reverence. Ordinances first instructed the people, and statutes then brought them into conformity, preserving an intention of reverent care and compassion in punishment. Thus, the excellence of the institutions was likewise no different from that of the Three Dynasties.
The laws through which the imperial ancestors founded the dynasty were already excellent. Thereafter, Emperor Renzong Zhao devoted himself resolutely to good government and entrusted men with wholehearted sincerity; Emperor Xuanzong Zhang laid aside warfare and cultivated civil affairs, bringing order to the five human relationships; and Emperor Yingzong Rui exercised the firmness of Heaven in making his own decisions and recovered his former possession of the throne. All diligently carried forward…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
守之傳至
陛下又能紹
列聖之憂勤守
祖宗之成法斯民樂育于熈皥之治者蓋已百二十
年雖三代治安之長久不是過矣
聖策乃謂治極而弛理勢自然
祖宗之良法美意豈能悉祗承而無弊臣知此固
聖人憂勤不已之心臣敢不備陳狂直以副
聖心之萬一乎臣惟法之立也本無不宜法之行也
始有其弊因其弊而救之則存乎其人古人有
===
言曰救弊者莫如脩德又曰救弊者莫如責實
臣愚竊謂今日救時之急務亦惟脩德責實益
致其勤而已蓋德者法之本也德之脩萬一有
不慎則其源之弊必至於縱欲以敗度譬之人
傷其氣而寒暑易侵木傷其根而風雨易折法
雖具也亦徒法而已矣實者名之主也實之責
萬一有不覈則其流之弊必至於欺謾以成風
譬之搏土為舟不足以利涉畫地為餅不足以
充饑名雖美也亦虛名而已矣故以舜之重華
協帝而伯益猶以罔失法度為言以舜之庶績

punctuated:
守之。傳至陛下，又能紹列聖之憂勤，守祖宗之成法，斯民樂育于熈皥之治者，蓋已百二十年，雖三代治安之長久，不是過矣。聖策乃謂：「治極而弛，理勢自然。祖宗之良法美意，豈能悉祗承而無弊？」臣知此固聖人憂勤不已之心。臣敢不備陳狂直，以副聖心之萬一乎？
臣惟法之立也，本無不宜；法之行也，始有其弊。因其弊而救之，則存乎其人。古人有言曰：「救弊者莫如脩德。」又曰：「救弊者莫如責實。」臣愚竊謂今日救時之急務，亦惟脩德責實，益致其勤而已。蓋德者，法之本也。德之脩，萬一有不慎，則其源之弊，必至於縱欲以敗度。譬之人傷其氣，而寒暑易侵；木傷其根，而風雨易折。法雖具也，亦徒法而已矣。實者，名之主也。實之責，萬一有不覈，則其流之弊，必至於欺謾以成風。譬之搏土為舟，不足以利涉；畫地為餅，不足以充饑。名雖美也，亦虛名而已矣。故以舜之重華協帝，而伯益猶以罔失法度為言；以舜之庶績
translation_en:
…preserved it. When the succession reached Your Majesty, you too carried forward the anxious diligence of the successive sage sovereigns and upheld the established laws of your ancestors. The people have now flourished happily under this bright and harmonious rule for some 120 years. Even the enduring peace and good government of the Three Dynasties did not surpass this. Yet your sagely policy question states: “When government reaches its height, it grows lax: this is the natural tendency of affairs. How can the fine laws and admirable intentions of our ancestors all be reverently upheld without abuses?” Your servant knows that this expresses the sage ruler’s unceasing concern and diligence. Dare I fail to set forth fully my rash and candid views, in hopes of answering even a ten-thousandth part of your sagely concern?
Your servant considers that laws, when established, are fundamentally appropriate; abuses arise only in their implementation. Remedying those abuses as they arise depends upon the people responsible. An ancient said: “For remedying abuses, nothing equals cultivating virtue.” Another said: “For remedying abuses, nothing equals demanding substance.” In my ignorance, I venture to suggest that the urgent task of remedying the troubles of our time likewise consists simply in cultivating virtue, demanding substance, and applying still greater diligence. Virtue is the foundation of law. If there is even the slightest lack of care in cultivating virtue, abuses at their source will inevitably lead to indulgence of desire and the ruin of established standards. This is like a person whose vital energy is injured and who is therefore readily assailed by cold and heat, or a tree whose roots are damaged and which is therefore readily broken by wind and rain. Though the laws remain complete, they are merely laws on paper. Substance is what gives a name its validity. If there is even the slightest failure to scrutinize matters when demanding substance, the resulting abuses will inevitably cause deceit to become customary. This is like molding earth into a boat, which cannot carry one safely across water, or drawing a cake on the ground, which cannot satisfy hunger. Though the name may be fine, it is merely an empty name. Thus, even though Shun’s renewed brilliance matched that of the emperor Yao, Bo Yi still urged him never to depart from laws and standards; and although Shun’s many achievements…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
咸熈而皐陶猶以屢省乃成為戒政以無虞之
世其脩德責實之功不可少怠耳今
陛下防非窒欲恪守舊章任賢使能大明黜陟所以
脩其德而責其實者固不可以有加矣而臣子
之心毎以有加無已而望
陛下此臣所以拳拳以勤為獻也況我
祖宗之法莫不以勤而創之臣嘗觀
祖宗之諭近臣有曰朕念創業之艱難日不暇食夜
不安枕又曰人君日理萬幾怠心一生則庶務
壅滯其患不可勝言又曰天下之大庶務之殷
===
豈可須臾怠惰一怠惰則百度弛矣凡此皆勤
之準的也
陛下既知惓惓以法
祖為念又可不法
祖宗之勤乎臣請以勤之說為
陛下別白而重言之夫君者天也天惟聰明剛健動
而不息是以其光為日月其文為星辰其威為
雷霆其澤為雨露而萬物之生於動者各得其
職天之行也一息有不繼則運動無常而不能
以宰萬物矣人君之御天下以其能憲天聰明

之準的也
