以宰萬物矣人君之御天下以其能憲天聰明
punctuated:
咸熈，而皐陶猶以屢省乃成為戒，政以無虞之世，其脩德責實之功不可少怠耳。今陛下防非窒欲，恪守舊章，任賢使能，大明黜陟，所以脩其德而責其實者，固不可以有加矣。而臣子之心，毎以有加無已而望陛下，此臣所以拳拳以勤為獻也。況我祖宗之法，莫不以勤而創之。臣嘗觀祖宗之諭近臣，有曰：「朕念創業之艱難，日不暇食，夜不安枕。」又曰：「人君日理萬幾，怠心一生，則庶務壅滯，其患不可勝言。」又曰：「天下之大，庶務之殷，豈可須臾怠惰？一怠惰，則百度弛矣。」凡此皆勤之準的也。陛下既知惓惓以法祖為念，又可不法祖宗之勤乎？臣請以勤之說為陛下別白而重言之。

夫君者，天也。天惟聰明剛健，動而不息，是以其光為日月，其文為星辰，其威為雷霆，其澤為雨露，而萬物之生於動者，各得其職。天之行也，一息有不繼，則運動無常，而不能以宰萬物矣。人君之御天下，以其能憲天聰明
translation_en:
…all flourished, yet Gao Yao still admonished him to review repeatedly what he had accomplished. Precisely because [?] it was an age free from anxiety, the work of cultivating virtue and demanding actual results could not be relaxed even slightly. Now Your Majesty guards against wrongdoing and restrains desire, scrupulously observes the established statutes, appoints the worthy and employs the capable, and makes dismissals and promotions manifestly clear. Your efforts to cultivate virtue and demand actual results surely admit of no further improvement. Yet your servants always look to Your Majesty for improvement without end. This is why I so earnestly offer diligence as my counsel. Moreover, every law of our imperial ancestors was founded through diligence. I have read their instructions to their close ministers. One says: “When I reflect on the difficulties of founding the dynasty, by day I have no leisure to eat, and at night I cannot rest easy on my pillow.” Another says: “The ruler attends daily to myriad affairs. Once an idle thought arises, all business becomes obstructed, and the resulting harm is beyond description.” Another says: “With all under Heaven so vast and its affairs so numerous, how can one be idle even for a moment? Once one becomes idle, all institutions fall into neglect.” These are all standards of diligence. Since Your Majesty already knows to keep earnestly in mind the emulation of your ancestors, can you fail to emulate their diligence as well? Allow me to explain clearly to Your Majesty the meaning of diligence and to speak of it once more.

The ruler is Heaven. Heaven is perceptive and discerning, firm and vigorous, moving without cease. Thus its radiance becomes the sun and moon, its patterns become the stars, its majesty becomes thunder, and its beneficence becomes rain and dew; and the myriad things born through its movement each fulfill their proper function. If Heaven’s course were interrupted for even a single breath, its movements would lose their constancy, and it could no longer govern the myriad things. The ruler governs all under Heaven because he can model himself on Heaven’s perceptiveness and discernment…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
體天剛健而惓惓焉勤勵不息也一或怠焉則
德有不脩實有不責先王之法委靡廢弛日趨
於弊而已又安能保天下之治哉臣願
陛下所其無逸罔或不動憲天之聰明以為聰明體
天之剛健以為剛健一念之萌必謹而察之曰
此於吾法得無有所害乎一令之出必反而思
之曰此於吾法得無有所紊乎無所害也無所
紊也然後從之不然不敢從也如是則人欲淨
盡天理昭融
聖德益脩而所以救弊者有其本矣由是條天下之
===
事其大者有幾表天下之人其可用者有幾鷄
鳴而起曰吾今日為某事用某人他日又曰吾
所為某事其事果濟矣乎所用某人其人果才
矣乎事果濟也人果才也然後已之不然不但
已也如是則為之而成革之而服名實相須而
所以救弊者有其要矣
陛下於是二者果能惓惓焉不違於心則勤之實以
盡內外百司群工庶職孰敢不仰體
陛下法
祖之心奮庸熈載恪守

punctuated: 體天剛健，而惓惓焉勤勵不息也。一或怠焉，則德有不脩，實有不責，先王之法委靡廢弛，日趨於弊而已，又安能保天下之治哉？臣願陛下所其無逸，罔或不動，憲天之聰明以為聰明，體天之剛健以為剛健。一念之萌，必謹而察之，曰：「此於吾法，得無有所害乎？」一令之出，必反而思之，曰：「此於吾法，得無有所紊乎？」無所害也，無所紊也，然後從之；不然，不敢從也。如是，則人欲淨盡，天理昭融，聖德益脩，而所以救弊者有其本矣。由是條天下之事，其大者有幾；表天下之人，其可用者有幾。鷄鳴而起，曰：「吾今日為某事，用某人。」他日又曰：「吾所為某事，其事果濟矣乎？所用某人，其人果才矣乎？」事果濟也，人果才也，然後已之；不然，不但已也。如是，則為之而成，革之而服，名實相須，而所以救弊者有其要矣。陛下於是二者，果能惓惓焉不違於心，則勤之實以盡。內外百司、群工庶職，孰敢不仰體陛下法祖之心，奮庸熈載，恪守
translation_en: …embodying Heaven’s strength and vigor, and earnestly exerting himself without cease. Should he become negligent even once, his virtue will go uncultivated and actual accomplishment will go unrequired; the laws of the former kings will languish, fall into disuse, and daily become more defective. How, then, could he preserve order throughout the realm? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would abide in freedom from ease, never failing to act, modeling your discernment upon Heaven’s discernment and embodying Heaven’s strength and vigor as your own. Whenever a thought first arises, carefully examine it, asking: “Might this in any way harm my laws?” Whenever an order is issued, reflect upon it, asking: “Might this in any way disrupt my laws?” Only when it causes neither harm nor disruption should you proceed with it; otherwise, do not venture to proceed. In this way, selfish human desires will be completely purged, Heaven’s principle will shine forth unobstructed, and your sagely virtue will be further cultivated. The remedy for abuses will thus have its foundation. From this basis, enumerate the affairs of the realm: how many are of major importance? Identify the men of the realm: how many are fit for employment? Rise at cockcrow and say: “Today I shall undertake this affair and employ this man.” On a later day, ask again: “Has the affair I undertook actually succeeded? Has the man I employed actually proved capable?” Only when the affair has truly succeeded and the man has truly proved capable should you let the matter rest; otherwise, do not simply let it rest [?]. In this way, what you undertake will be accomplished, the changes you make will win compliance, and names and realities will accord with one another. You will thus possess the essentials for remedying abuses. If Your Majesty can indeed attend earnestly to these two things, never allowing them to depart from your heart, the substance of diligence will be fully realized. Among the many offices within and outside the capital, and all their officials and functionaries, who would dare fail reverently to embody Your Majesty’s resolve to emulate your ancestors, exert themselves in service, bring their duties to fruition, and scrupulously observe …

典訓而慎行之乎？以是守祖宗之紀綱，必能開衆正之門，杜群枉之路，威福得以專而無侵撓之患，政事得以脩而無阿私之失。以是守祖宗之統體，必能存仁厚之風，行寛大之政，垂旒黈纊而黙其聰察，藏疾納汙而務於包涵。以是守祖宗之制度，必能惜名器，公用舍，以精吏治；必能重師儒，慎科貢，以正士風。理財也，必能罷無名之征，停不急之務；理兵也，必能稽私役之卒，懲賄求之將；禮樂則必能革奢僭之習，放淫哇之聲；刑政則必能除慘刻之科，重威富之罰。將見弊無不興，弊無不補，今日之急務無不治，良法美意可以祗承，而無偏失不舉、名存實爽之議。由是而吏稱其職，由是而民安其業，由是中國尊而四夷服，由是風雨時而嘉祥至。凡陛下所期，無不如志，可以保盈成於萬世之久，可以躋至治於三代之上矣。區區漢唐宋之功業，烏足言哉！

translation_en:
…the canonical instructions and carefully put them into practice? By thus preserving the guiding principles of your ancestors, Your Majesty will surely open the way for all upright men and bar the paths of the wicked. The authority to punish and reward will remain exclusively yours, free from encroachment or obstruction, and government affairs will be put in order without favoritism or private bias. By thus preserving the overall framework of your ancestors’ rule, you will surely sustain a spirit of benevolence and generosity and enact lenient policies. With the pendants of your crown hanging before your eyes and the yellow floss beside your ears, you will refrain from displaying your acuity in hearing and seeing; you will tolerate faults and bear with impurities, striving for forbearance. By thus preserving your ancestors’ institutions, you will surely guard the honors and insignia of office and act impartially in appointments and dismissals, thereby improving official administration. You will surely esteem Confucian teachers and exercise care in examinations and the recommendation of scholars, thereby rectifying scholarly conduct. In managing finances, you will surely abolish unjustified levies and suspend nonessential undertakings. In managing the military, you will surely investigate the use of soldiers for private service and punish commanders who seek advancement through bribes. In ritual and music, you will surely reform extravagant and presumptuous practices and banish licentious and debased sounds. In penal administration, you will surely eliminate cruel provisions and impose heavier punishments upon the powerful and wealthy [?]. You will then see every abuse brought to flourishing [?] and every defect repaired, and all the urgent affairs of the present properly managed. Excellent laws and worthy intentions can be reverently upheld, without grounds for criticism that they are unevenly applied, neglected, or preserved in name while violated in substance. Thus officials will fulfill their duties; thus the people will pursue their livelihoods in peace; thus the Central Realm will be honored and the peoples of the four quarters submit; thus wind and rain will come in season and auspicious signs appear. Everything Your Majesty hopes for will accord with your wishes. You can preserve the fullness of established achievement for ten thousand generations and raise perfect government above that of the Three Dynasties. How could the paltry achievements of the Han, Tang, and Song merit mention!

Such, in broad outline, is what Your Majesty has asked your servant in the policy question. At its conclusion, you further ask: “You scholars who study antiquity, comprehend the Classics, and aspire to serve the world should each state frankly…”

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
以對無有所隱且寵之以
朕將親覽之一言臣荷
陛下生成之德沐
陛下教養之恩學雖不足以通經而志於用世也久
矣今幸一登
文石之陛涉
赤墀之塗承
問而對臣之職也直言無隱臣之忠也况
陛下導臣而使之言哉臣復有一言以為
陛下獻者惟欲
===
陛下終始此勤而已昔周公之於成王有無逸之戒
宋璟之於玄宗亦有無逸之圖二臣之言初非
有異二君之治乃有不同蓋成王聽周公之言
而無間故卒致鳧鷖之休玄宗用宋璟之言而
不終故卒成天寶之禍是則人君之治莫不興
於勤而廢於逸人君之勤鮮克善其始而慎其
終此前代彰灼著明之效有國者不可以不慎
也伏願
陛下以成王為法以玄宗為戒以臣之言為不欺慎
終如始不敢逸豫則

translation_en:
…in reply, concealing nothing.” Moreover, Your Majesty honored us with the words, “I shall personally read them.” Your servant has received Your Majesty’s life-giving and nurturing beneficence and enjoyed Your Majesty’s gracious instruction and cultivation. Though my learning is insufficient to comprehend the Classics, I have long aspired to serve the world. Now, fortunate enough to ascend the patterned stone steps and tread the vermilion court, I fulfill my duty as your servant by answering the question put to me; by speaking frankly and concealing nothing, I demonstrate my loyalty. How much more should I do so when Your Majesty encourages me to speak! Your servant has one further word to offer Your Majesty: I wish only that Your Majesty sustain this diligence from beginning to end.
In former times, the Duke of Zhou admonished King Cheng with Against Idleness; Song Jing likewise presented Emperor Xuanzong with an Illustration of Against Idleness. The two ministers’ words were no different in principle, yet the two rulers’ governments differed in their results. King Cheng heeded the Duke of Zhou’s words without interruption and thus ultimately attained the blessings celebrated in Wild Ducks and Gulls. Xuanzong followed Song Jing’s words but failed to persist to the end, and thus ultimately brought about the calamity of the Tianbao era. Thus, rulers’ governments invariably flourish through diligence and fall into ruin through idleness; yet few rulers can begin their diligence well and remain heedful to the end. These are the plainly manifest results of earlier ages, which those who rule a state must consider with care. I humbly pray that Your Majesty take King Cheng as a model and Xuanzong as a warning, accept your servant’s words as truthful, remain as heedful at the end as at the beginning, and never presume to indulge in idle ease; then…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
臣劉春
臣對臣聞置大器者固貴乎建大法尤貴乎正
大本夫天下大器也紀綱統體制度大法也而
人君一心則大本也凡器之在人置得其地則
安失其地則危况天下者莫大之器而置之可
以無法乎然法固置天下之具使不本於心則
推之不準動之不化欲置是器於安全之域又
可得乎故古之人君不患器之未安也而惟恐
法不能立不患法之未立也而惟恐心不能正
心得其正則以之建法足以行於萬世而無弊
===
以之守法足以衍於無疆而有光夏商周所以
隆一代之治者固此心之正也漢唐宋所以不
能繼三代之隆者庸非此心之正有未純乎宋
儒程子以為為政須要有綱紀文章朱子曰天
下之事其本在於一人而一人之身其本在於
一心即此意也欽惟
皇帝陛下聰明睿智孝友温恭有寬仁博愛之度有
神武不殺之威負荷
祖宗之大器恪守
祖宗之大法海宇乂安黎民醇厚所以置大器固若

punctuated:
臣劉春。
臣對：臣聞置大器者，固貴乎建大法，尤貴乎正大本。夫天下，大器也；紀綱統體制度，大法也；而人君一心，則大本也。凡器之在人，置得其地則安，失其地則危。况天下者，莫大之器，而置之可以無法乎？然法固置天下之具，使不本於心，則推之不準，動之不化，欲置是器於安全之域，又可得乎？故古之人君，不患器之未安也，而惟恐法不能立；不患法之未立也，而惟恐心不能正。心得其正，則以之建法，足以行於萬世而無弊；以之守法，足以衍於無疆而有光。夏商周所以隆一代之治者，固此心之正也；漢唐宋所以不能繼三代之隆者，庸非此心之正有未純乎？宋儒程子以為，為政須要有綱紀文章。朱子曰：「天下之事，其本在於一人；而一人之身，其本在於一心。」即此意也。
欽惟皇帝陛下，聰明睿智，孝友温恭，有寬仁博愛之度，有神武不殺之威，負荷祖宗之大器，恪守祖宗之大法，海宇乂安，黎民醇厚，所以置大器，固若
translation_en:
Your servant Liu Chun.
Your servant replies: I have heard that, in establishing the great vessel, it is indeed important to institute great laws, but still more important to rectify the great foundation. All under Heaven is the great vessel; its guiding principles, overarching organization, and institutions are the great laws; and the ruler’s single heart is the great foundation. Any vessel in human hands is secure when placed where it belongs, and endangered when placed where it does not. How, then, could All under Heaven, the greatest of vessels, be established without laws? Yet although laws are the means of establishing All under Heaven, if they are not rooted in the heart, their application will lack a proper standard and their operation will fail to transform the people. Could one then hope to place this vessel in safety? Thus the rulers of antiquity worried less that the vessel was not yet secure than that laws could not be established, and less that laws were not yet established than that their hearts could not be rectified. Once the heart is rectified, laws established through it can operate for ten thousand generations without harmful consequences; laws upheld through it can endure without limit and shine with glory. It was indeed this rectitude of heart that enabled the Xia, Shang, and Zhou to bring the government of their respective ages to greatness. Was the failure of the Han, Tang, and Song to continue the greatness of the Three Dynasties not due to some lack of purity in this rectitude of heart? The Song Confucian Master Cheng held that government must have guiding principles, discipline, and articulated institutions. Master Zhu said: “The affairs of All under Heaven have their foundation in one person; and that person’s own being has its foundation in a single heart.” This is precisely what they meant.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor is perceptive and sagacious, filial and affectionate toward your brothers, gentle and reverent. You possess the magnanimity of generous benevolence and universal love, and the awe-inspiring power of divine martial prowess that has no need to kill. You bear the great vessel entrusted by your imperial ancestors and scrupulously uphold their great laws. The realm is orderly and peaceful, and the common people are sincere and virtuous. Thus the great vessel you have established is as firm as …

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
泰山磐石而無阽危之患矣然猶不自滿假
廷集多士諏咨治道始欲聞創業守成之得失終
欲究今時急務之所在顧臣愚陋曷能仰揆
淵衷然竊嘗觀唐虞之時治固至矣而君臣之間
未嘗以已治自足故大禹陳克艱之戒伯益陳
儆戒之謨舜之作歌也亦曰勅天之命惟時惟
幾君臣之間豈故私憂過計哉盖當泰之時而
審復隍之戒居豫之時而存介石之心此治安
之效所以有隆無替也
陛下當熈洽之時而動問察之念深惟法
祖為心則所以保盈成之運躋至治之道在是矣臣
復何言臣惟
陛下有是心也而力於行則
宗社億萬年無疆之休也謹拜手稽首對揚
休命之萬一臣聞自古帝王創造丕圖必有貽謀
以為長治久安之計而其謀之貽也有紀綱焉
有統體焉有制度焉合而言之皆法也紀綱者
法之大端所以總攝人心統體者法之大分所
以包括治具制度者法之條目則所以為僭擬
之防而顯然於典章文物之間者耳有紀綱而

之防而顯然於典章文物之間者耳有紀綱而
punctuated:
泰山磐石，而無阽危之患矣。然猶不自滿假，廷集多士，諏咨治道，始欲聞創業守成之得失，終欲究今時急務之所在。顧臣愚陋，曷能仰揆淵衷？然竊嘗觀唐虞之時，治固至矣，而君臣之間未嘗以已治自足，故大禹陳克艱之戒，伯益陳儆戒之謨。舜之作歌也，亦曰：「勅天之命，惟時惟幾。」君臣之間豈故私憂過計哉？盖當泰之時而審復隍之戒，居豫之時而存介石之心，此治安之效所以有隆無替也。陛下當熈洽之時而動問察之念，深惟法祖為心，則所以保盈成之運、躋至治之道在是矣。臣復何言？臣惟陛下有是心也，而力於行，則宗社億萬年無疆之休也。謹拜手稽首，對揚休命之萬一。

…as secure as Mount Tai and a massive rock, free from the danger of collapse. Yet Your Majesty remains unsatisfied with your achievements. You have assembled the many scholars at court to consult them about the way of government, asking first to hear of successes and failures in founding a dynasty and preserving its accomplishments, and finally to investigate the urgent tasks of the present day. But how could your ignorant and uncultivated servant fathom your profound intentions? Nevertheless, I have reflected that in the time of Tang and Yu, government had indeed attained perfection, yet neither ruler nor ministers ever considered existing good order sufficient. Thus Da Yu offered his admonition about recognizing the difficulty of rule, and Bo Yi presented his counsel urging vigilance. When Shun composed his song, he too said: “Be heedful of Heaven’s mandate; attend to the times and to the first signs of change.” Were ruler and ministers deliberately indulging in private anxieties and excessive calculations? Surely, in a time of peace they considered the warning that the city wall might fall back into its moat; amid ease they maintained a resolve firm as rock. This is why their achievements in good government and peace flourished without decline. In this time of prosperity and harmony, Your Majesty is moved to inquire and investigate, taking deeply to heart the emulation of your ancestors. Herein lies the means of preserving this era of fullness and accomplishment and advancing toward perfect government. What more can your servant say? I hold only that, if Your Majesty possesses this resolve and strives to put it into practice, it will bring boundless blessings to the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain for countless ages. Reverently bowing with my hands together and touching my forehead to the ground, I respond to and extol even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command.
Your servant has heard that, from ancient times, emperors and kings who founded a great dynastic enterprise invariably left plans to their successors, providing for lasting good government and enduring peace. These plans comprised guiding principles, an overarching framework, and institutions and regulations. Taken together, all of these constitute governing norms. Guiding principles are the chief elements of these norms, through which people’s hearts are brought together and held in order. The overarching framework consists of their major divisions, encompassing the instruments of government. Institutions and regulations are their detailed provisions, guarding against the presumptuous imitation of one’s superiors and finding visible expression in statutes, ceremonial forms, and cultural institutions. title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
後能一天下之勢有統體而後能正天下之治
有制度而後能制天下之情人君貽治安之計
於後世盖未有舍此者書曰有典有則貽厥子
孫詩曰詒厥孫謀以燕翼子是已臣請舉三代
之槩言之夏之興也禹以克勤克儉之德膺舜
曆數之傳商之興也湯以聖敬日躋之德舉弔
民伐罪之師周之興也武王以建其有極之德
定文王未集之統其受命也皆天人之協應其
立法也皆精義之所存所謂紀綱統體制度盖
纖悉兼備矣觀其惇敘九族而文命四敷克寬
===
克仁而萬邦表正惇信明義而彝倫攸敘忠質
文之異尚渾渾然寬大淳厚之風子丑寅之迭
建蕩蕩乎正大光明之業田以養民也有曰貢
曰助曰徹之異學以教民也有曰校曰序曰庠
之殊禮有三禮五禮及禮儀三百所以節民性
者無不具樂有大夏大濩及大武之章所以和
民心者無或闕兵足以禦侮而無陸梁之患刑
足以禁奸而無枉撓之失是其紀綱以振而內
外相維也統體以立而規模弘遠也制度精密
而鉅細無遺也禹湯文武創造於前者如此及

translation_en:
…only then can the forces of the realm be united. Only with an overarching order can the realm’s governance be set right; only with institutions and regulations can the dispositions of the realm’s people be regulated. No ruler who bequeathed to later generations a plan for good government and peace has ever dispensed with these. The Book of Documents says: “There are established institutions and rules to bequeath to his descendants.” The Book of Odes says: “He bequeaths plans to his descendants, thereby bringing peace to and assisting his children.” This is precisely the point. Your servant asks leave to discuss the broad outlines of the Three Dynasties.

When the Xia arose, Yu, through his virtue of diligence and frugality, received the succession to the heavenly mandate transmitted by Shun. When the Shang arose, Tang, through his sagely reverence and daily advancement in virtue, raised an army to succor the people and punish the guilty. When the Zhou arose, King Wu, through his virtue in establishing the supreme standard, secured the dynastic succession that King Wen had not yet brought to completion. In receiving the mandate, all enjoyed the concordant response of Heaven and humankind; in establishing laws, all embodied the finest principles of rightness. What we call guiding principles, overarching order, and institutions and regulations were thus complete in every detail.

Consider how they ordered the nine degrees of kinship with generous affection, so that civil instruction spread in all directions; how they practiced magnanimity and benevolence, so that the myriad states took them as their model and were set right; and how they upheld trustworthiness and made righteousness manifest, so that the enduring human relationships were properly ordered. Though they differed in their esteem for loyalty, simplicity, and refinement, their prevailing spirit was abundantly generous, broad, sincere, and substantial. Though they successively designated the months associated with zi, chou, and yin as the beginning of the year, their undertakings were grand, upright, and luminous.

Fields served to nourish the people, with different arrangements called gong, zhu, and che—tribute, assistance, and common levy. Schools served to teach the people, with different establishments called xiao, xu, and xiang. Ritual included the three rites, the five rites, and the three hundred ceremonial observances: everything needed to regulate the people’s dispositions was provided. Music included the compositions Great Xia (Da Xia), Great Huo (Da Huo), and Great Wu (Da Wu): nothing needed to harmonize the people’s hearts was lacking. Armed forces sufficed to repel aggression, without the menace of rampant violence; punishments sufficed to restrain wrongdoing, without the faults of injustice or perversion of the law.

Thus their guiding principles were put into effect, and the inner and outer domains sustained one another; their overarching order was established, and the scope of government was broad and far-reaching; their institutions and regulations were precise and thorough, omitting nothing great or small. Such were the foundations laid earlier by Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu; and when…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
其嗣世之君欲繩祖武以隆景運亦惟率循舊
典雖或乆也不能無偏而不舉之處則興滯補
弊期使斯民得被先王之澤而已固非有加於
典則之外焉如啟之恭行天罰大戰於甘高宗
恭默思道嘉靖殷邦周宣側身脩行任賢使能
是皆興滯補弊也卒之有扈以之而蕩滅蠻夷
重譯而来朝海內翕然而向風上足以紹烈祖
之耿光下有以致時雍之盛治則其奮勵有為
之實不亦槩可見乎三代而後嬴秦暴虐無足
論矣漢高帝豁達大度寬厚長者如列置郡縣
===
===
分設刺史而規摹優裕約法三章剖符封功而
寬大不苛以至叔孫通制禮儀韓信脩軍法享
祀有樂均田有制亦云可矣然井田壞而不能
復學校廢而不能脩與凡兵刑禮樂之事雖具
而亦多襲嬴秦之舊則其紀綱統體制度臣未
敢以為得也語其嗣世如文帝之躬脩玄默絕
意遊畋宣帝之綜核名實信賞必罰固當時賢
君也惜其禮樂未遑而教化有不備刑名繩下
而德教有未純功業果足稱乎自漢而後三國
鼎峙六朝瓜分無足論矣唐太宗負英武之資

===
分設刺史而規摹優裕約法三章剖符封功而
寛大不苛以至叔孫通制禮儀韓信脩軍法享
祀有樂均田有制亦云可矣然井田壞而不能
復學校廢而不能脩與凡兵刑禮樂之事雖具
而亦多襲嬴秦之舊則其紀綱統體制度〔臣未〕
敢以為得也語其嗣世如文帝之躬脩玄默絶
意遊畋宣帝之綜核名實信賞必罰固當時賢
君也惜其禮樂未遑而教化有不備刑名繩下
而德教有未純功業果足稱乎自漢而後三國
鼎峙六朝瓜分無足論矣唐太宗負英武之資
punctuated:
其嗣世之君欲繩祖武以隆景運，亦惟率循舊典。雖或乆也，不能無偏而不舉之處，則興滯補弊，期使斯民得被先王之澤而已，固非有加於典則之外焉。如啟之恭行天罰，大戰於甘；高宗恭默思道，嘉靖殷邦；周宣側身脩行，任賢使能，是皆興滯補弊也。卒之有扈以之而蕩滅，蠻夷重譯而来朝，海內翕然而向風。上足以紹烈祖之耿光，下有以致時雍之盛治，則其奮勵有為之實，不亦槩可見乎？
三代而後，嬴秦暴虐，無足論矣。漢高帝豁達大度，寬厚長者。如列置郡縣，分設刺史，而規摹優裕；約法三章，剖符封功，而寬大不苛；以至叔孫通制禮儀，韓信脩軍法，享祀有樂，均田有制，亦云可矣。然井田壞而不能復，學校廢而不能脩，與凡兵刑禮樂之事，雖具而亦多襲嬴秦之舊，則其紀綱、統體、制度，臣未敢以為得也。語其嗣世，如文帝之躬脩玄默，絕意遊畋；宣帝之綜核名實，信賞必罰，固當時賢君也。惜其禮樂未遑，而教化有不備；刑名繩下，而德教有未純。功業果足稱乎？
自漢而後，三國鼎峙，六朝瓜分，無足論矣。唐太宗負英武之資
translation_en:
…their successor rulers, wishing to follow their ancestors’ footsteps and bring their glorious fortunes to greater flourishing, likewise did no more than adhere to the established precedents. Although, with the passage of time, some matters inevitably became unbalanced or fell into neglect, they revived what had stalled and remedied abuses, seeking only to let the people receive the beneficence of the former kings. They certainly added nothing beyond the established norms. Thus Qi reverently executed Heaven’s punishment and fought the great battle at Gan; Gaozong remained reverently silent, contemplating the Way, and brought good order and peace to the state of Yin; and King Xuan of Zhou conducted himself with circumspection, cultivated his conduct, appointed the worthy, and employed the capable. All these were instances of reviving what had stalled and remedying abuses. In consequence, the Youhu were utterly destroyed; the Man and Yi came to court through successive interpreters; and all within the seas unanimously submitted to the rulers’ influence. They were thus able, above, to carry forward the brilliant glory of their illustrious ancestors and, below, to achieve flourishing government in universal harmony. Does this not allow us to discern, in broad outline, the substance of their vigorous and purposeful efforts?
After the Three Dynasties, the Qin of the Ying house was cruel and tyrannical, and merits no discussion. Emperor Gao of Han was open-minded and magnanimous, a generous and kindly elder. He established commanderies and counties throughout the realm and separately appointed Regional Inspectors, giving his arrangements ample scope; he reduced the laws to three articles and divided tallies to enfeoff those who had rendered meritorious service, acting generously and without harshness. Moreover, Shusun Tong established ceremonial observances, Han Xin developed military regulations, music accompanied sacrificial offerings, and there were regulations for equalizing the distribution of land. These achievements may indeed be judged creditable. Yet the well-field system had broken down, and he could not restore it; the schools had fallen into disuse, and he could not rehabilitate them. Although arrangements existed for military affairs, punishments, rites, and music, these too largely followed the old practices of the Qin of the Ying house. Thus, as to his governing principles, overall organization, and institutions, I, your servant, dare not consider them properly established. Among his successors, Emperor Wen personally cultivated profound quietude and renounced excursions and hunting, while Emperor Xuan comprehensively examined whether actual performance matched professed responsibilities, rewarded reliably, and punished without fail. They were certainly worthy rulers of their time. Regrettably, they found no time for rites and music, leaving moral instruction incomplete; they used penal and administrative standards to discipline their subordinates, while their teaching through virtue remained impure. Do their accomplishments truly merit praise?
After the Han, the Three Kingdoms stood opposed like the legs of a tripod, and under the Six Dynasties the realm was partitioned like a melon; these merit no discussion. Emperor Taizong of Tang possessed a heroic and martial disposition…

懷安民之志如周典建官府衛置兵而法令嚴
察備定律令禁笞鞭背而仁厚攸存以至建立
學校增廣生員口分世業以均田租庸調法以
定賦亦云可矣然雅樂作而不免於俗音顯慶
禮制而皆雜以式令與凡兵刑教養之事雖具
而亦未復先王之制則其紀綱統體制度臣未
敢以為得也語其嗣世如玄宗之勵精政事任
賢納諫憲宗之志平僭叛能用忠謀亦當時令
主也惜其奸佞干政而致乗輿之播遷信任非
人而罹不測之逆禍功業果足論乎自唐而五
===
季壞亂極矣宋祖隆興削平僭國以文臣處藩
鎮以杯酒釋兵權藹然禮義之化不容苛虐哀
矜無辜温然忠厚之風重農務本則田里以均
興學崇儒則祠宇增葺以至兵有三衙四廂之
制刑有大辟覆奏之典固英仁之主也然刑雖
制而未能懲贓吏之犯兵雖設而未能復幽燕
之地凡其教養禮樂之事亦皆議論多而成功
少則其紀綱統體制度抑豈能如三代者哉迨

宗之聰明英毅銳志恢復庶幾守成之君也然

懷安民之志，如周典建官，府衛置兵，而法令嚴察；備定律令，禁笞鞭背，而仁厚攸存。以至建立學校，增廣生員，口分世業以均田，租庸調法以定賦，亦云可矣。然雅樂作而不免於俗音，顯慶禮制而皆雜以式令，與凡兵刑教養之事雖具，而亦未復先王之制，則其紀綱統體制度，臣未敢以為得也。語其嗣世，如玄宗之勵精政事，任賢納諫；憲宗之志平僭叛，能用忠謀，亦當時令主也。惜其奸佞干政，而致乗輿之播遷；信任非人，而罹不測之逆禍。功業果足論乎？自唐而五季，壞亂極矣。

…cherished the resolve to bring peace to the people. He established offices after the institutions of Zhou and stationed troops in military prefectures and guards [?], enforcing laws and ordinances strictly. He comprehensively established penal statutes and administrative ordinances and prohibited beating or whipping the back, thus preserving benevolence and generosity. He also established schools, increased student numbers, equalized landholding through per-capita allotments and hereditary holdings, and fixed taxation through the system of grain tax, labor service or its commutation, and textile levy. These measures, too, may be called acceptable. Yet although court ritual music was composed, it remained tainted by popular melodies; the ritual institutions of the Xianqing era were all intermixed with administrative regulations and ordinances. Although provisions for military affairs, punishments, education, and nurture were in place, they still failed to restore the institutions of the former kings. As for his governing framework and overall institutional order, your servant therefore dares not consider them sound. Among his successors, Xuanzong devoted himself energetically to government, employed worthy men, and accepted remonstrance; Xianzong resolved to suppress usurpers and rebels and could act on loyal counsel. They, too, were excellent rulers of their times. Regrettably, treacherous flatterers interfered in government, causing the imperial carriage to flee and wander; trust was placed in the wrong men, bringing unforeseen calamity through treason. Were their achievements truly worthy of praise? From the Tang to the Five Dynasties, disorder and ruin reached their utmost extent.

The founding emperor of the Song rose to greatness and subdued the usurping states. He placed civil officials in charge of regional military commands and, over cups of wine, relieved commanders of their military authority: a gracious transformation through ritual propriety and righteousness. He tolerated no harsh oppression and pitied the innocent: a gentle spirit of loyalty and generosity. By valuing agriculture and attending to the foundation of livelihood, he brought equitable arrangements to the fields and villages. By promoting learning and honoring Confucian scholars, he enlarged and repaired shrines. In military affairs, moreover, there was the system of the Three Commands and Four Divisions; in penal affairs, there was the rule requiring death sentences to be resubmitted to the throne for review. He was assuredly a valiant and humane ruler. Yet although punishments were established, they failed to check the offenses of corrupt officials; although military forces were organized, they failed to recover the lands of You and Yan. In education, nurture, rites, and music, likewise, there was much discussion but little accomplishment. How, then, could his governing framework and overall institutional order compare with those of the Three Dynasties? Among his successors, Renzong was reverent, frugal, benevolent, and forbearing, employing all the worthy men; Xiaozong was intelligent, valiant, and resolute, firmly bent on recovering the lost territory. They came close to being rulers who preserved the achievements they had inherited. Yet…

…there was an excess of benevolence and gentleness, yet the alien peoples inflicted insults unchecked; the lost territories remained unrecovered, and the dynasty, content with its restricted domain, failed to rally. Were their achievements really worthy of discussion? The rulers of the Three Dynasties established institutions that attained complete excellence, and their successors likewise achieved deeds of energetic and purposeful action. The rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song established institutions that fell short of complete excellence, and their successors likewise lacked achievements worthy of praise. That the former attained complete excellence was not without a source: it rested upon the rectitude of the hearts of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. That the latter fell short of complete excellence had no other cause: it rested upon the hearts of the Han founder, the Tang sovereign, and the Song founder not being wholly upright. As for succeeding rulers, some revived what had languished and remedied defects, bringing glory to their predecessors; others accommodated themselves to crude and makeshift arrangements, leaving no renown to posterity. Was this not also because some had upright hearts and others did not?
We reverently reflect that Taizu, the Gao Emperor, rose like a dragon in the Huai region and unified all the realm. He revived the cardinal bonds and constant moral norms after their collapse, and opened heaven and earth anew in an act of restoration. At the center he established commissions and ministries to administer governmental affairs as a whole; in the provinces he established Provincial Administration Commissions and Provincial Surveillance Commissions to administer the territories separately. Officials were charged with remonstrance and entrusted with serving as his ears and eyes; official responsibilities were differentiated, and duties were strictly defined. To nourish the people, he reiterated the orders concerning uncultivated land; to educate scholars, he enforced the regulations inscribed on the recumbent stelae. He commanded Niu Liang to formulate rites to stabilize the people's resolve, and Tao Kai to direct music to harmonize their hearts. Selection and training followed sound methods, so troops were never insufficient; statutes and substatutes provided standards, so penal administration was invariably clear. His plans were detailed and lucid, all embodying sound institutions and benevolent intentions; his regulations were precise and thorough, all containing profound benevolence and abundant beneficence. His guiding principles, overarching organization, and institutions—the means by which the great vessel of sovereignty was securely established—truly accorded with those of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, though they lived in different ages, and were to be revered for ten thousand generations.

…the texts of the [Six] Classics. His grand plans and far-reaching strategies brought glory to his predecessors and ample provision for his successors. The successive sage emperors further enhanced this work of continuation: civil and military officials rendered effective service, and the people and all living things attained peace. These achievements truly sufficed to rival the distant flourishing of the Three Dynasties, leaving the Han, Tang, and Song inferior by comparison.
Yet Your Majesty says that when good government reaches its height, laxity follows as a natural tendency of affairs, and that the ancestral laws cannot all be reverently upheld without abuses. You therefore wish to observe the canonical instructions scrupulously and implement them carefully, giving no grounds for criticism that they are applied partially or incorrectly, left unenforced, or preserved in name while betrayed in substance. You thereby hope that officials will fulfill their duties, the people will pursue their livelihoods in peace, the Central Kingdom will be honored and the peoples of the four quarters will submit, winds and rains will arrive in season, and auspicious signs will appear. Upon reverently reading this far, your servant can glimpse Your Majesty’s earnest desire to emulate your ancestors: to remedy present abuses and secure the stability of the sovereign realm, bringing glory to your ancestors through your achievements and bequeathing your great undertaking to your descendants. How great are the sovereign’s words! How single-minded is the sovereign’s heart! Here indeed lies the means to prolong the dynasty’s enduring destiny and increase the blessings of the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain.
Yet your servant has reflected quietly upon this. The canonical instructions of our imperial ancestors encompass the refined and the coarse, the great and the small, with nothing omitted: the laws have already been established. But after a long period of peace, abuses arise alongside the laws, just as Your Majesty fears. In the countryside, the scourge of land engrossment persists; in the schools, habits of frivolity and extravagance persist. The army serves to repel aggression, yet it constantly lacks brave soldiers; punishments serve to prohibit violence, yet many people continually suffer injustice and oppression. Extravagance exceeds proper bounds and usurps the privileges of higher rank, while customs that honor fundamentals and attend to substance are rare. Music incites desire and increases sorrow [?], while harmonious, peaceful, serene, and restrained tones are seldom heard. These are all urgent matters of the present day …

translation_en:
…among the most important. The other matters that violate principle and impede government cannot readily be enumerated one by one. In general, although the laws of the imperial ancestors are fully established, those who carry them out may have fallen short. This is why they still burden Your Majesty with cares that keep you occupied before dawn and until late at night. What other course can there be now? In my humble opinion, it lies solely in Your Majesty’s rectifying your mind. Consider how the Duke of Zhou composed “Establishing Government” to instruct King Cheng: everything he set forth concerned appointing officials and employing men, yet he invariably placed settling the mind first. This was truly because the mind is the great foundation of all under Heaven, from which every transformation proceeds. Thus, if the mind is not correct, the great foundation is not established; the guiding principles of government cannot be reinvigorated, its overarching structure cannot be established, and its institutions cannot be made clear. Even if one wishes to speak of good government, everything amounts only to expedients. Yet the mind, subtle as it is, comes under attack from a multitude of desires.
Your Majesty’s sagely wisdom is lofty and clear, your refinement and singleness of purpose uninterrupted; certainly, depravity and delusion cannot move you. Nevertheless, if the work of nurturing, guarding, and sustaining the mind suffers even a slight interruption, the mind cannot help losing its rectitude. The Song Confucian scholar Zhen Dexiu said: “Only learning can nourish this mind; only reverence can preserve this mind; only drawing close to exemplary men can sustain this mind.” I venture to say that nothing is more essential than this to the way of rectifying the mind.
Your Majesty frequently attends the Classics Colloquium and continually illuminates your sagely learning; your learning is assuredly consummate. I humbly hope that, in the time remaining after holding court, you will also study at leisure and absorb these teachings fully. Let the Six Classics, the works of the philosophers and historians, the Precious Instructions of the imperial ancestors, and the books compiled by successive sage emperors all be set beside you daily for your reading. …advancing day by day and month by month, through learning attaining ever greater illumination: this is what those words mean.
Your Majesty sits with hands folded in the court, your mind abiding in profound stillness: your reverence is indeed consummate. I humbly wish that, even when resting, you will invariably remain dignified and respectful. Do not compose your bearing in the great court yet indulge yourself in the inner palace, or constrain yourself when in the company of worthy men yet become careless when alone. Then you will be as awestruck as though divine powers were above you, with no admixture of wrongful or perverse thoughts, and this mind will be preserved. The Book of Documents says, “Let the king make reverence his abiding place; he must not fail to revere virtue.” This is what those words mean.
When Your Majesty holds court, the dukes and ministers attend around you: you certainly keep the company of gentlemen. I humbly wish that, in the private halls as well, you will carefully select ministers of literary learning and choose men of circumspection and integrity to attend you in your leisure and be available for consultation. Let them enlighten your mind as occasion offers, so that loyal words reach your ears each day, and offer admonition as matters arise, so that pernicious doctrines do not confuse your mind. Then this mind will be sustained. The Commentary says, “By habitually dwelling with upright men, one cannot fail to become upright [?].” This is what those words mean.
If this is so, Your Majesty’s mind, already bright as the sun, will grow brighter still; already clear as water, it will grow clearer still. Before it is stirred by external things, there will be not the slightest bias; once it has issued into activity, there will be not the slightest error. This will manifest itself in employing men and conducting government, and become evident in issuing commands and promulgating orders. The guiding principles of government will be invigorated, without the danger of neglect or laxity; its unified structure will be established, without encroachment or disruption; and its institutions will be made clear, without violations or usurpations. Consequently, all the offices within and outside the capital, and officials of every rank and function, will scrupulously uphold and carefully implement the statutes and instructions of your imperial ancestors. translation_en: …left unimplemented, or of things surviving in name while their substance is lost? Your servant dwells obscurely among the common people, utterly ignorant and of humble station. Reverently receiving your enlightened edict, I have throughout offered the rectification of the mind as my counsel, fully aware that this is the commonplace talk of Confucian scholars. Yet nothing is more essential than this to the establishment of good government by emperors and kings or to the teachings handed down by sages and worthies. Mencius said: “Unless it is the Way of Yao and Shun, I dare not set it forth before the king.” Your servant studies Confucius and Mencius: how could I dare fail to offer the Way of Yao and Shun to my sovereign? If only Your Majesty would not dismiss this as commonplace talk, but deign to give it a little of your sagely attention, all under Heaven would be most fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

text:
臣涂瑞
臣對臣聞前王之垂統者當有以立其法後王
之繼統者當有以守其法皆本乎一心之誠而
已盖法莫大乎紀綱統體制度也然非誠于内
而致行之力則立之也弗善守之也弗堅如是
而欲國統之延長不可得矣故前王之立法必
誠心以立之而後可以垂統于後後王之守法
必誠心以守之而後可以繼統于前夏商周所
以統緒相承無有窮已者以其立法守法之本
於誠也漢唐宋所以不古若者豈非立之守之
===
者徒有其法而無其誠歟然則立法者固本於
誠矣而守法者又可不誠其心乎孟子曰徒法
不能以自行子思曰惟天下至誠為能參天地
贊化育良以此也伏惟
皇帝陛下聰明睿知有聖人之資孝友謙恭有聖人
之德所以保盈成而躋至治至矣盡矣不可以
有加矣然猶舉行盛典志切求賢乃進臣等於
廷俯賜清問諮之以法
祖之事責之以盡言之忠所謂智周萬物而一得之
愚不棄威加四海而芻蕘之賤必詢者也臣雖

臣涂瑞。
臣對：臣聞前王之垂統者，當有以立其法；後王之繼統者，當有以守其法。皆本乎一心之誠而已。盖法莫大乎紀綱、統體、制度也。然非誠于内而致行之力，則立之也弗善，守之也弗堅。如是而欲國統之延長，不可得矣。故前王之立法，必誠心以立之，而後可以垂統于後；後王之守法，必誠心以守之，而後可以繼統于前。夏商周所以統緒相承，無有窮已者，以其立法守法之本於誠也。漢唐宋所以不古若者，豈非立之守之者徒有其法而無其誠歟？然則立法者固本於誠矣，而守法者又可不誠其心乎？孟子曰：「徒法不能以自行。」子思曰：「惟天下至誠，為能參天地，贊化育。」良以此也。
伏惟皇帝陛下，聰明睿知，有聖人之資；孝友謙恭，有聖人之德。所以保盈成而躋至治，至矣，盡矣，不可以有加矣。然猶舉行盛典，志切求賢，乃進臣等於廷，俯賜清問，諮之以法祖之事，責之以盡言之忠。所謂智周萬物而一得之愚不棄，威加四海而芻蕘之賤必詢者也。臣雖

Your servant Tu Rui.
Your servant replies: I have heard that former kings who handed down their succession must have had means to establish their laws, and later kings who inherited that succession must have had means to uphold those laws. Both rest solely upon sincerity of heart. For nothing in law is more important than the guiding principles of government, its overarching structure, and its institutions and regulations. Yet without inward sincerity and strenuous effort in implementation, laws will neither be well established nor firmly upheld. To seek the prolongation of the dynastic succession under such conditions is impossible. Thus, former kings establishing laws had to do so with sincere hearts before they could transmit their succession to later generations; later kings upholding laws had to do so with sincere hearts before they could continue the succession of their predecessors. The reason the Xia, Shang, and Zhou transmitted their dynastic lines in unbroken succession was that their establishment and maintenance of laws rested on sincerity. Was it not because those who established and upheld laws under the Han, Tang, and Song possessed only the laws, without sincerity, that these dynasties fell short of antiquity? If establishing laws assuredly rests upon sincerity, can those who uphold them fail to make their hearts sincere? Mencius said: “Laws alone cannot put themselves into practice.” Zisi said: “Only those of utmost sincerity under Heaven can form a triad with Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nurturing work.” This is precisely the reason.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses the natural endowments of a sage in your intelligence and discerning wisdom, and the virtues of a sage in your filial devotion, fraternal affection, humility, and reverence. Your efforts to preserve the fullness of established achievement and attain the highest order of government have reached such perfection and completeness that nothing could be added. Yet you still conduct this grand ceremony, earnestly intent upon seeking worthy men. You have therefore brought us, your servants, into the court and graciously bestowed your august questions upon us, consulting us on the task of following your ancestors’ example and requiring the loyalty of speaking our minds fully. This is what is meant by wisdom that encompasses all things yet does not discard the single insight of a fool, and authority that extends over the Four Seas yet invariably consults even humble gatherers of grass and firewood. 休命乎臣惟天下之治固在於法天下之法必本
於心法者治之具法有不立不足以為治心者
法之本心有不誠不可以立法故自古帝王創

之大者傳曰紀綱既正天下大定又曰體統正

punctuated:
愚賤，敢不極慮，昧死以對揚休命乎？臣惟天下之治固在於法，天下之法必本於心。法者，治之具；法有不立，不足以為治。心者，法之本；心有不誠，不可以立法。故自古帝王創造丕圖，必立法貽謀，以為長治久安之計。而紀綱統體制度，所以防範人心、維持家國，皆貽謀之大者。傳曰：「紀綱既正，天下大定。」又曰：「體統正而朝廷尊。」又曰：「制度一而風俗同。」皆是意也。然其法之立也，要必本之於誠耳。臣請以三代立法之君言之。

禹以方懋厥德，繼舜而興。當時彞倫攸敘，而文命四敷；克勤克儉，而不自滿假。曰典曰則，貽後有謀；曰校曰貢，教養有法。此夏之紀綱統體制度也。

湯以天錫勇智，繼夏而王。當時人紀肇脩，而式于九圍；克寬克仁，而彰信兆民。三風十愆，官有常儆；八家九區，田有定畫。此商之紀綱統體制度也。

…ignorant and lowly though I am, dare I fail to exert my utmost thought and, risking death, respond to and extol your gracious command? Your servant considers that governing All-under-Heaven indeed depends upon laws, and that the laws of All-under-Heaven must be rooted in the heart. Laws are the instruments of government: unless they are established, they cannot suffice for governing. The heart is the foundation of laws: unless it is sincere, laws cannot be established. Thus, from antiquity, whenever emperors and kings founded their great enterprises, they invariably established laws and bequeathed plans to their successors, making provision for enduring good government and lasting peace. The governing principles, institutional order, and regulations by which they restrained people’s hearts and sustained the ruling house and state were all major elements of these bequeathed plans. The transmitted texts say, “Once the governing principles are rectified, All-under-Heaven is firmly settled.” They also say, “When institutional order is correct, the court is held in honor,” and, “When regulations are uniform, customs are alike.” All express this meaning. Yet the establishment of these laws must, above all, be rooted in sincerity. Allow your servant to illustrate this through the lawgiving rulers of the Three Dynasties.

Yu, vigorously cultivating his virtue, succeeded Shun and rose to power. In his time, the enduring human relationships were set in order, and his civilizing instructions spread to the four quarters. He was diligent and frugal, without becoming conceited or complacent. Through canons and rules, he bequeathed plans to posterity; through schools and the tribute system, he provided methods for educating and sustaining the people. Such were the governing principles, institutional order, and regulations of Xia.

Tang, endowed by Heaven with courage and wisdom, succeeded Xia and became king. In his time, the bonds of human relationships were restored and became a model throughout the nine regions. He was magnanimous and benevolent, manifesting his trustworthiness to the multitudes. Against the three corrupt habits and ten faults, officials had standing admonitions; with eight households and nine plots, agricultural land had fixed divisions. Such were the governing principles, institutional order, and regulations of Shang.

As for King Wen, through his admirable gentleness and excellent reverence, he laid the foundation of an enterprise that possessed two-thirds of the realm. King Wu, through his resolute strength and illustrious achievements, completed the sovereign enterprise still unfinished after nine years. Consider how they followed the enduring teachings and cultivated harmony throughout the Chinese realm; how they esteemed the five teachings of human relationships and graciously pacified the four quarters; how they bestowed kindness and relief upon widowers and widows, bringing all the people into harmony; and how they eliminated the cruel and removed the violent, so that the myriad people gladly submitted. text:
千三百之條其建學以教民則有曰庠制產以
養民則有曰徹此周之紀綱統體制度也夫三
代立法之善如此非自善也本於禹湯文武心
乎誠耳使禹不能允執厥中湯不能咸有一德
文武不能純亦不已細行亦矜則其所貽之謀
隨立隨仆曷有傳於後乎三代而下之創業者
若漢祖唐宗宋祖亦知立法以垂統矣然其心
之誠者有未至故其法之立者亦有未善以言
乎高祖規模宏遠而大綱攸立然呂氏專權而
政由房闥也寬仁愛人而大體以正然養成諂
===
諛而國祚以衰也雖律令禮儀成於蕭何叔孫
章程軍法定於張蒼韓信然襲秦之弊曾何足
齒以言乎太宗法令分明而蠻夷率服然宮闈
瀆亂民無所則也嚴明英武而深知治體然好大
喜功勤兵於遠也雖貞觀之禮成於玄齡魏徵
學校之化及於高麗百濟然襲隋之舊又烏足
道至若宋之太祖忠厚廉耻大綱攸正然國勢
不振王道未醇也道德仁義無讓漢唐然惠褻
而威不振賞數而加無功雖制禮也則因陋就
簡而禮之制紛紜雖作樂也則黨同伐異而樂

千三百之條。其建學以教民，則有曰庠；制產以養民，則有曰徹。此周之紀綱統體制度也。夫三代立法之善如此，非自善也，本於禹湯文武心乎誠耳。使禹不能允執厥中，湯不能咸有一德，文武不能純亦不已、細行亦矜，則其所貽之謀，隨立隨仆，曷有傳於後乎？

三代而下之創業者，若漢祖唐宗宋祖，亦知立法以垂統矣。然其心之誠者有未至，故其法之立者亦有未善。以言乎高祖，規模宏遠，而大綱攸立；然呂氏專權，而政由房闥也。寬仁愛人，而大體以正；然養成諂諛，而國祚以衰也。雖律令禮儀成於蕭何叔孫，章程軍法定於張蒼韓信，然襲秦之弊，曾何足齒？以言乎太宗，法令分明，而蠻夷率服；然宮闈瀆亂，民無所則也。嚴明英武，而深知治體；然好大喜功，勤兵於遠也。雖貞觀之禮成於玄齡魏徵，學校之化及於高麗百濟，然襲隋之舊，又烏足道？至若宋之太祖，忠厚廉耻，大綱攸正；然國勢不振，王道未醇也。道德仁義，無讓漢唐；然惠褻而威不振，賞數而加無功。雖制禮也，則因陋就簡，而禮之制紛紜；雖作樂也，則黨同伐異，而樂
translation_en:
…thousand three hundred provisions. In establishing schools to educate the people, there were those called xiang; in regulating their livelihoods to sustain them, there was the system called che. These were the guiding principles, overall structure, and institutions of Zhou. The laws established by the Three Dynasties were excellent in this way, yet their excellence did not arise of itself: it was rooted simply in the sincerity of the hearts of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. Had Yu been unable truly to hold fast to the mean, Tang unable consistently to possess a single virtue, and Wen and Wu unable to remain unceasingly pure and attend carefully even to minor acts, the plans they bequeathed would have collapsed as soon as they were established. What could then have been transmitted to posterity?

Among those who founded dynasties after the Three Dynasties, Gaozu of Han, Taizong of Tang, and Taizu of Song also understood how to establish laws and bequeath a ruling tradition. Yet because the sincerity of their hearts fell short, the laws they established likewise fell short of excellence. To speak of Gaozu: his designs were broad and far-reaching, and the main framework was established. Yet the Lü clan monopolized power, and government proceeded from the inner apartments. He was generous, humane, and loving toward others, and the essentials of government were set right. Yet he fostered flatterers, and the dynasty’s fortunes consequently declined. Although statutes, ordinances, and ceremonial observances were completed by Xiao He and Shusun, and administrative regulations and military laws were settled by Zhang Cang and Han Xin, they perpetuated the defects of Qin. How could they deserve mention?

To speak of Taizong: his laws and ordinances were clear, and the foreign peoples submitted. Yet within the palace there was moral defilement and disorder, leaving the people without an example to follow. He was strict, discerning, heroic, and martial, and deeply understood the essentials of government. Yet he delighted in grand undertakings and coveted achievements, exhausting his troops in distant lands. Although the rites of the Zhenguan reign were completed by Xuanling and Wei Zheng, and the transforming influence of schools reached Gaoli and Baiji, they perpetuated the old practices of Sui. How, again, could they merit discussion?

As for Taizu of Song, he upheld loyalty, generosity, integrity, and a sense of shame, and the main framework was set right. Yet the power of the state remained weak, and the Kingly Way was not pure. In moral virtue, humaneness, and righteousness, he yielded nothing to Han or Tang. Yet favors became commonplace and authority failed to assert itself; rewards were frequent and bestowed upon those without merit. Although rites were instituted, existing inadequacies were accepted and expedient simplifications adopted, leaving ritual institutions confused. Although music was created, men sided with those who agreed with them and attacked those who differed, and music…

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
之說雜亂取士以浮文失先王作養之意歛民
非一端失先王中正之法夫禹湯文武以誠而
立法其得如彼漢祖唐宗宋祖不以誠而立法
者其失如此則前王之垂統不可不本於誠矣
先王之立法固本於誠迨其嗣世之君欲保盈
成以躋至治一惟力體先王之誠遵用先王之
典其或久也不能無偏而不舉之處則亦興滯
補弊期使斯民得被先王之澤而後已也臣請
以三代守法之君言之禹之後有啓時則有扈
陸梁威侮五行怠棄三正禹之業幾於墜矣啓
===
賢能敬承繼禹之道大召六卿恭行天討以成
謳歌之化有夏之業於是而復振湯之後有高
宗時則鬼方負固毒亂一隅三年不庭湯之業
幾於隳矣高宗起而復湯之業整肅軍士敬行
天罰以臻嘉靖之休商之令緒於是而有光文
武之後有宣王則能側身脩行任賢使能北伐
玁狁南征荊蠻而文武之境土以復之數君皆
奮發有為之主夫豈無自而然盖有誠心以為
之本也使啓不能敬承高宗不能恭默宣王不
能脩行則盈成之運隨補隨漏曷有光於前乎

謳歌之化有夏之業於是而復振湯之後有高
宗時則鬼方負固毒亂一隅三年不庭湯之業

奮發有爲之主夫豈無自而然蓋有誠心以爲

punctuated:
之說雜亂。取士以浮文，失先王作養之意；歛民非一端，失先王中正之法。夫禹湯文武以誠而立法，其得如彼；漢祖唐宗宋祖不以誠而立法者，其失如此。則前王之垂統，不可不本於誠矣。
先王之立法，固本於誠。迨其嗣世之君欲保盈成以躋至治，一惟力體先王之誠，遵用先王之典。其或久也，不能無偏而不舉之處，則亦興滯補弊，期使斯民得被先王之澤而後已也。臣請以三代守法之君言之。
禹之後有啓，時則有扈陸梁，威侮五行，怠棄三正，禹之業幾於墜矣。啓賢能，敬承繼禹之道，大召六卿，恭行天討，以成謳歌之化，有夏之業於是而復振。湯之後有高宗，時則鬼方負固，毒亂一隅，三年不庭，湯之業幾於隳矣。高宗起而復湯之業，整肅軍士，敬行天罰，以臻嘉靖之休，商之令緒於是而有光。文武之後有宣王，則能側身脩行，任賢使能，北伐玁狁，南征荊蠻，而文武之境土以復之。數君皆奮發有為之主，夫豈無自而然？盖有誠心以為之本也。使啓不能敬承，高宗不能恭默，宣王不能脩行，則盈成之運隨補隨漏，曷有光於前乎？
translation_en:
…the theories of music were confused. They selected officials on the strength of superficial literary ornament, losing sight of the former kings’ intention to nurture talent; they exacted levies from the people in many ways, departing from the former kings’ balanced and upright methods. Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu established institutions with sincerity, and their achievements were as described above; the founding emperor of Han, Taizong of Tang, and the founding emperor of Song established institutions without sincerity, and their failings were such as these. Thus, when earlier kings bequeathed their dynastic succession, they could not dispense with sincerity as its foundation.
The former kings’ establishment of institutions was indeed founded upon sincerity. When their successors wished to preserve the prosperity already achieved and attain the highest order of government, their sole course was earnestly to embody the former kings’ sincerity and follow their established institutions. Over time, there would inevitably be aspects that had become unbalanced or fallen into neglect. They therefore revived what had languished and remedied defects, not resting until the people could enjoy the benefits bestowed by the former kings. Your servant asks leave to illustrate this with rulers of the Three Dynasties who upheld their inherited institutions.
After Yu came Qi. At that time, the Youhu defiantly rose up, brazenly affronting the Five Phases and neglecting and abandoning the Three Standards of calendrical order. Yu’s accomplishments were almost lost. Worthy and capable, Qi reverently upheld and continued Yu’s Way. He summoned the six ministers in a great assembly and reverently carried out Heaven’s punitive expedition, bringing to fruition a transforming influence celebrated in song. Thus the enterprise of the Xia was revitalized. After Tang came Gaozong. At that time, the Guifang relied on their strong defenses, wreaking havoc in one region and refusing for three years to render submission at court. Tang’s accomplishments were almost destroyed. Gaozong arose to restore Tang’s enterprise, imposed order and discipline upon his troops, and reverently carried out Heaven’s punishment, attaining the blessings of good order and peace. Thus the splendid legacy of the Shang gained new luster. After Wen and Wu came King Xuan. He humbled himself and cultivated his conduct, appointed the worthy and employed the capable, attacked the Xianyun in the north, and campaigned against the Jingman in the south, thereby recovering the territories of Wen and Wu. These rulers were all energetic sovereigns who accomplished much. Could this have happened without a source? It was because they had sincere hearts as their foundation. Had Qi been unable reverently to carry on his inheritance, Gaozong unable to maintain reverent silence, and King Xuan unable to cultivate his conduct, then the prosperity they inherited would have sprung fresh leaks with every repair. How could they have brought glory to their predecessors?

title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
三代而下之守成者若漢宣帝唐玄宗宋仁宗
亦知守法以繼統然其心之誠者或有所雜故
其法之守者亦有未堅彼宣帝起自閭閻知民
疾苦即位之初勵精為治使吏稱民安光前裕
後其功業似可稱者惜乎欺詐雜出而啓亡漢
之釁擇術不精而雜申韓之流玄宗相父起兵
聿定大難開元之初憂勤庶政使海內富庶四
夷賓服其功業有可稱者惜乎侈心一動而縱
遊娛聲色之好奸諛並進而貽生靈社稷之患
至若仁宗之恭儉仁恕敬天重民常服浣濯之
===
衣不極膏梁之味時則政無貪殘獄皆平允又
功業之可稱者惜乎郭后一事於德有疵慶曆
諸賢不終其用夫夏啓商宗周宣能以誠而守
法其盡善也如彼宣帝玄宗仁宗不以誠而守
法其庶幾也如此則後王之繼統者又不可不
本於誠矣洪惟我

三代而下之守成者，若漢宣帝、唐玄宗、宋仁宗，亦知守法以繼統，然其心之誠者或有所雜，故其法之守者亦有未堅。彼宣帝起自閭閻，知民疾苦，即位之初，勵精為治，使吏稱民安，光前裕後，其功業似可稱者。惜乎欺詐雜出，而啓亡漢之釁；擇術不精，而雜申韓之流。玄宗相父起兵，聿定大難，開元之初，憂勤庶政，使海內富庶，四夷賓服，其功業有可稱者。惜乎侈心一動，而縱遊娛聲色之好；奸諛並進，而貽生靈社稷之患。至若仁宗之恭儉仁恕，敬天重民，常服浣濯之衣，不極膏梁之味，時則政無貪殘，獄皆平允，又功業之可稱者。惜乎郭后一事，於德有疵；慶曆諸賢，不終其用。夫夏啓、商宗、周宣，能以誠而守法，其盡善也如彼；宣帝、玄宗、仁宗，不以誠而守法，其庶幾也如此。則後王之繼統者，又不可不本於誠矣。
洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝，以聖智之資而奄一寰宇；太宗文皇帝，以神武之畧而中靖邦家。其心，一禹湯文武之心；其法，一禹湯文武之法。若
translation_en:
Among those who preserved the achievements of their predecessors after the Three Dynasties, Emperor Xuandi of Han, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, and Emperor Renzong of Song also understood that they must uphold established laws to carry on the imperial succession. Yet their sincerity of heart was sometimes mingled with other motives, and thus their adherence to those laws was not always firm. Xuandi rose from among the common people and knew their hardships. At the beginning of his reign, he devoted himself energetically to good government, ensuring that officials fulfilled their duties and the people lived in peace. He brought glory to his predecessors and provided generously for posterity; his accomplishments seem worthy of praise. Regrettably, deceit and fraud also appeared, opening the breach that would lead to the fall of Han; his insufficient discernment in choosing methods of rule allowed the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei to enter into his government. Xuanzong assisted his father in raising troops and thereby quelled a great crisis. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, he attended diligently and anxiously to the many affairs of government, bringing wealth and abundance within the seas and securing the submission of the peoples beyond the frontiers. His accomplishments were worthy of praise. Regrettably, once his desire for extravagance stirred, he indulged his taste for recreation, music, and sensual pleasures. Treacherous flatterers advanced together, bringing calamity upon the people and the dynasty. As for Renzong, he was reverent, frugal, benevolent, and forbearing; he revered Heaven and valued the people. He regularly wore washed garments and did not indulge to the utmost in rich delicacies. In his time, government was free of greed and cruelty, and judicial decisions were all fair and equitable. Here too were accomplishments worthy of praise. Regrettably, the affair of Empress Guo blemished his virtue, and he failed to retain the services of the worthy men of the Qingli era to the end. Qi of Xia, Gaozong of Shang, and King Xuan of Zhou could uphold established laws through sincerity: such was their consummate excellence. Xuandi, Xuanzong, and Renzong upheld established laws without grounding themselves in sincerity: such was their mere approximation to that excellence. Later rulers who inherit the imperial succession must therefore likewise take sincerity as their foundation.
We reverently reflect that our dynasty’s Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, possessed sagely wisdom and united all under Heaven; Taizong, the Cultured Emperor, possessed divinely martial strategic ability and pacified the realm within. title: 成化二十三年進士登科錄
text:
大誥申明五常之典六經表章性理之學立同姓
婚娶之禁革山川王侯之號則紀綱無不正也
以寬大為德有君臣同遊之條以勤儉為規嚴
萬民奢靡之禁則統體無不正也養民有田足
國有賦而田賦之制新興學有方取士有道而
學校之制立凡若此者又非制度之善乎
祖宗貽謀既本乎一心之誠自是而後若
仁宗昭皇帝
宣宗章皇帝
英宗睿皇帝又皆以聖紹聖益隆繼述盈成之治所
===
以超漢唐軼有宋而追跡於三代者又莫不本
乎一心之誠也仰惟
陛下受天命之攸歸嗣
祖宗之大業即位以來優禮大臣以禮義為紀綱不
事小察以寬大為統體親臨太學而注意於造
士躬耕籍田而用心於養民斯世斯民樂熈皥
之天享太平之福已餘二紀于兹矣然
祖宗良法美意行之既久人情漸玩民偽漸滋弊因
以生誠有如
聖策所慮者臣聞繩祖武以受天祜武王所以繼於

婚娶之禁華山川王侯之號則紀綱無不正也
以寬大為德有君臣同遊之條以勤儉為規嚴
萬民奢靡之禁則統體無不正也養民有田足
國有賦而田賦之制新興學有方取士有道而
學校之制立凡若此者又非制度之善乎
祖宗貽謀既本乎一心之誠自是而後若
仁宗昭皇帝
宣宗章皇帝
英宗睿皇帝又皆以聖繼聖益隆繼述盈成之治所
===
以超漢唐軼有宋而追跡於三代者又莫不本
乎一心之誠也仰惟
陛下受天命之攸歸嗣
祖宗之大業即位以來優禮大臣以禮義為紀綱不
事小察以寬大為統體親臨太學而注意於造
士躬耕籍田而用心於養民斯世斯民樂熙皡
之天享太平之福已餘二紀于茲矣然
祖宗良法美意行之既久人情漸玩民偽漸滋弊因
以生誠有如
聖策所慮者臣聞繩祖武以受天祜武王所以繼於
punctuated:
《大誥》申明五常之典，六經表章性理之學，立同姓婚娶之禁，革山川王侯之號，則紀綱無不正也。以寬大為德，有君臣同遊之條；以勤儉為規，嚴萬民奢靡之禁，則統體無不正也。養民有田，足國有賦，而田賦之制新；興學有方，取士有道，而學校之制立。凡若此者，又非制度之善乎？
祖宗貽謀，既本乎一心之誠，自是而後，若仁宗昭皇帝、宣宗章皇帝、英宗睿皇帝，又皆以聖紹聖，益隆繼述盈成之治。所以超漢唐、軼有宋，而追跡於三代者，又莫不本乎一心之誠也。
仰惟陛下受天命之攸歸，嗣祖宗之大業，即位以來，優禮大臣，以禮義為紀綱；不事小察，以寬大為統體；親臨太學，而注意於造士；躬耕籍田，而用心於養民。斯世斯民，樂熈皥之天，享太平之福，已餘二紀于兹矣。然祖宗良法美意，行之既久，人情漸玩，民偽漸滋，弊因以生，誠有如聖策所慮者。臣聞，繩祖武以受天祜，武王所以繼於
translation_en:
…the Great Pronouncements clarified the enduring norms of the Five Constant Virtues, and the Six Classics gave prominence to the learning of human nature and principle. Marriage between people of the same surname was prohibited, and the titles of prince and marquis conferred upon mountains and rivers were abolished. Thus the guiding principles of government were all set right. Magnanimity was esteemed as a virtue, with provisions for ruler and ministers to enjoy excursions together; diligence and frugality were made the rule, with strict prohibitions against extravagance among the people. Thus the overall framework of government was all set right. There were fields to sustain the people and taxes to provide for the state, and the system of land taxation was renewed. There were methods for promoting learning and proper means of selecting officials, and the school system was established. Were not all these instances of excellent institutions?
The plans bequeathed by the imperial ancestors were already rooted in wholehearted sincerity. Thereafter, Emperor Renzong Zhao, Emperor Xuanzong Zhang, and Emperor Yingzong Rui each succeeded a sage as a sage himself, further enhancing the governance that carried forward their predecessors’ achievements and preserved their flourishing accomplishments. Their surpassing the Han and Tang, outstripping the Song, and following in the footsteps of the Three Dynasties were likewise all rooted in wholehearted sincerity.
I reverently consider how Your Majesty received Heaven’s mandate as the one to whom it rightly devolved and inherited the great enterprise of the imperial ancestors. Since ascending the throne, you have treated your high ministers with exceptional courtesy, making ritual propriety and righteousness the guiding principles of government. You have refrained from scrutinizing petty matters, making magnanimity its overall framework. You have personally visited the Imperial University, devoting attention to cultivating scholars, and plowed the imperial ritual field yourself, setting your mind upon nourishing the people. The people of this age have rejoiced beneath a heaven of radiant harmony and enjoyed the blessings of peace for more than twenty-four years. Yet, as the excellent laws and worthy intentions of the imperial ancestors have been put into practice over a long period, people have gradually grown heedless, deceit among the populace has gradually increased, and abuses have consequently arisen. These are indeed such as Your Majesty’s policy question expresses concern about. Your servant has heard that following in his ancestors’ footsteps to receive Heaven’s blessing was how King Wu succeeded …

text:
文兼三王而施四事公旦所以忠於周書曰監
于先王成憲其永無愆詩曰不愆不忘率由舊
章則今日之急務亦惟存誠以守法而已盖誠
者真實無妄之謂三代之法貴實不貴名誠故
也今日之法所以偏失不舉名存實爽者
陛下之誠非不至也而奉行者或未得其要歟臣願
陛下體
祖宗列聖之誠守
祖宗列聖之法興滯補弊而勤勵不息循名責實而
虛偽不齒如紀綱之實或不能無紊亂之失也
===
則必誠以守之使九疇必敘四維必張足以興
起乎人心綱維乎世教不可徒徇紀綱之名焉
統體之實或不能無變更之失也則必誠以守
之使道德必醇風俗必厚足以培養乎元氣靈
長乎
社稷不可徒徇統體之名焉至於制度之立則又
必以誠而守之如田賦也必實足以養民學校
也必實足以教民又豈可徒徇其名而不責其
實哉如是則內外百司百工庶職各守其分各
安其職居丞弼之任者以能論道德和陰陽居

…King Wen. Drawing together the ways of the Three Kings and putting the four matters into practice was how Dan, Duke of Zhou, showed his loyalty to Zhou. The Book of Documents says: “Look to the established statutes of the former kings, and you will forever be without error.” The Book of Odes says: “Neither erring nor forgetting, follow the old institutions.” Thus the urgent task today is simply to preserve sincerity and thereby uphold the laws. Sincerity means being true and genuine, without falsehood. The laws of the Three Dynasties valued substance rather than name because they rested on sincerity. If today’s laws are unevenly applied or left unenforced, surviving in name while their substance is lost, it is not that Your Majesty’s sincerity is deficient. Might those who carry them out have failed to grasp their essentials?

Your servant wishes Your Majesty to embody the sincerity of your ancestors, the successive sage emperors, and uphold their laws; to revive what has fallen into disuse and remedy abuses with unremitting diligence; and to demand performance commensurate with names and exclude the false and pretentious. If the actual operation of governing principles and discipline cannot be entirely free of disorder, you must uphold them with sincerity, ensuring that the Nine Categories are duly ordered and the Four Bonds are firmly extended, sufficiently to rouse people’s hearts and sustain moral instruction throughout the realm. You must not merely pursue governing principles and discipline in name. If the substance of the overarching order cannot be entirely free of harmful alteration, you must uphold it with sincerity, ensuring that morality is pure and customs are sound, sufficiently to nourish the realm’s vital energy and secure the enduring vitality of the altars of soil and grain. You must not merely pursue that overarching order in name.

As for the establishment of institutions, these too must be upheld with sincerity. Land taxation must truly suffice to nourish the people, and schools must truly suffice to educate them. How could one merely pursue their names without demanding substantive results? In this way, the many offices at court and beyond, and officials in every kind of post, will each observe their proper responsibilities and attend securely to their duties. 財計之司者，必能通有無、足國用；諫官必直言得失，臺臣必彈戢愆違；藩臬勵其職於一方，守令勵其職於郡縣。有奮庸熈載之休，無偏失不舉之可議；有恪守典訓之美，無名存實爽之可非。吏稱其職，民安其業，國勢尊安，四夷之遠於是而咸賓，風雨順時，諸福之祥於是而畢至。三代雍熈泰和之治復見於今日，而漢唐宋事功之陋，豈足言哉！雖然，守法固本於誠，而存誠尤有其要。

translation_en:
…those in charge of fiscal administration must be able to circulate resources between places of abundance and scarcity and provide adequately for the state's expenditure. Remonstrance officials must speak frankly about successes and failures, and censorial officials must impeach and restrain misconduct. Provincial Administration and Surveillance Commissioners must diligently discharge their duties within their regions, and prefects and magistrates within their prefectures and counties. There will be the excellence of vigorous service and flourishing accomplishments, with no grounds for criticism of partiality, error, or neglected duties; there will be the virtue of scrupulously observing the canonical instructions, with no grounds for reproaching a mere preservation of names that belies the reality. Officials will fulfill their responsibilities, and the people will pursue their livelihoods in peace. The state will be honored and secure, and even the distant barbarians of the four quarters will all submit. Wind and rain will come in due season, and auspicious signs of every blessing will arrive together. The harmonious, flourishing, and peaceful government of the Three Dynasties will appear again today. How could the paltry achievements of the Han, Tang, and Song merit mention? Nevertheless, although upholding established laws rests fundamentally upon sincerity, preserving sincerity has its own essential requirement.
Why does Your Majesty not consider the Way of Heaven? The primal vital force, regardless of antiquity or the present, cold or heat, wind, rain, or darkness, has circulated constantly through all ages, never stopping for even a single breath: this is Heaven's substance, wholly grounded in sincerity. The things under Heaven, whether vast or minute, great or small, flying or submerged, moving or standing still, have continually come into being through all ages, without a single thing deviating from its proper order: this is Heaven's functioning, wholly grounded in sincerity. Great indeed is sincerity! In Heaven it is real principle; in human beings it is a true heart. What makes Heaven Heaven is this real principle. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would model yourself upon Heaven to preserve this true heart, remaining watchful over yourself when alone in a dark room where no one sees you, and preserving your heart in times of thunderous utterance and profound silence. When compassion arises, let it be unmixed with malice or harmful intent; when shame and aversion to wrongdoing arise, let them be unmixed with greed or benightedness. Thereby expand benevolence and [illegible]…

之心，而不可勝用。當其辭讓之發，而不餒於險慆；當其是非之發，而不雜於昏惑，于以充禮智之量，而無少間斷。一念之動，必隨念察之，使無一念之或妄；一事之行，必隨事察之，使無一事之或雜。大廷深宫，地有異也，必彼此一誠，而勿貳以二；居處與人，事有殊也，必動靜一誠，而勿參以三。若然，則人欲日消，天理日明。陛下所存之德，即天德也；所行之道，即天道也。將見紀綱統體制度之在天下者，如一元之氣不息，而四時行焉；如五行之運不雜，而萬物生焉。尚何祖宗之法有不能持守也哉？
臣學不足以待問，才不足以應變，惟因聖問所及，謹直述以對。若夫騁浮文以取容，摭陳言以希寵，則非臣之志，亦非陛下策士求言之心也。倘蒙少垂采納，則國家幸甚，天下幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the heart, making its resources inexhaustible. When feelings of deference arise, let them not be weakened by perversity and excess [?]; when the sense of right and wrong arises, let it not be mingled with confusion and delusion. Thus enlarge your capacity for ritual propriety and wisdom without the slightest interruption. Whenever a thought stirs, examine that thought, allowing none to be misguided; whenever an action is undertaken, examine that action, allowing none to be adulterated. The great court and the secluded palace differ in location, but in both maintain the same sincerity, without dividing it in two. Dwelling in private and dealing with others differ in circumstance, but in activity and stillness maintain the same sincerity, without fragmenting it into three. If this is done, selfish desires will diminish daily, and Heaven’s principle will become clearer daily. The virtue Your Majesty preserves will be Heaven’s virtue; the Way you practice will be Heaven’s Way. Then the guiding principles, the overarching order, and the institutions throughout the realm will resemble the ceaseless primordial vital force through which the four seasons proceed, and the orderly operation of the Five Phases through which the myriad things are born. What laws of your imperial ancestors could then prove impossible to uphold?
Your servant’s learning is insufficient to answer your inquiries, and his ability insufficient to respond to changing circumstances. I have merely followed the matters raised in your sagely questions and respectfully answered them with a straightforward account. To parade empty literary ornament to gain acceptance, or to gather stale sayings in hopes of favor, is neither your servant’s intention nor Your Majesty’s purpose in examining scholars through policy questions and seeking their counsel. If you should graciously adopt even a little of this advice, it would be a great blessing for the state and for all under Heaven. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
